text:
Bugs aren't done — yet. In the future, I believe any vulnerability in code will be exploited almost instantly by bots. But any program has a finite number of bugs, and the defender gets to search it first and for as long as they want before release. AI helps make that search exhaustive, and with formal methods we can probably prove code bug-free. This favors the defender.

Obviously, we need to change how we ship software, and the transition will be challenging. But the end result is good.

text:
10月24日追踪 $BTC

最近盘面有点拧：买盘动能在减弱、卖盘在加强，Coinbase 溢价也一直偏折价——美盘情绪不算好。但价格到了 8 万出头就是跌不太下去。

我的判断｜这更像「有人想砸、但砸不深」的焦灼区，不是单边崩盘启动。下跌如果来，更可能是后面更好拉的筹码整理；真正阴跌，要么要有利空配合插针，要么情绪差到一定程度。

中期选举这块，逻辑其实很直接：
川普政府对加密是友好的。若竞选过程里参众两院都丢，市场会偏悲观——后面法案更难推，友好总统也会被卡住；丢一个，态度偏中性。偏悲观的路径，会给主力一个「走一波下跌」的可选窗口，最近流动性、美债、原油也都有点紧。

但很多人已经把这个账算明白了。所以 8 万出头、甚至 79500 附近已经有人在接。从筹码峰看，这个成本带堆得很厚——即便再往下探，也容易很快被拉回来。

链上提醒｜现价 ±5% 成本带的供应集中度（10/22 日线）已经到 16.99%，标在危险区域。前一日大约 15.3%，几天前还在 14.5% 一带；看板显示卡在 13% 高度警戒以上已经 16 天。白话讲：越多筹码挤在现价附近，小波动就会改更多人的盈亏状态——积累越厚，后面一旦方向选边，波动会很剧烈。

微观结构上也能对上：
Coinbase 溢价 24H 均值大约 -0.14%（10/23 15:00 UTC），接近极端折价，说明美元盘相对偏弱。
同时挂单侧，8 万出头反复有人在买——昨晚币安合约 80800 附近看到大约 600 BTC 量级的大单，到了位置我也在群里说过可以做多；但到 82000 又顶不动。所以现在是「下面有人接、上面过不去」的僵持。

我怎么看｜中期选举叙事提供的是「可跌的借口」，不是已经确认的下跌趋势。现阶段更值得盯的是：8 万出头这带筹码还加不加厚、82000 有没有量能突破、以及有没有真正把情绪打穿的利空。

接下来盯这三件事：
1）供应集中度日线是否继续往 17%+ 堆，还是高位回落
2）4H 能否带量收上 82000；收不上去就继续当焦灼区
3）Coinbase 溢价是否从极端折价修复；持续深折价 = 美盘情绪还没回来

text:
I’m genuinely in two minds about the abliterated model debate. It boils down to a liberty v paternalism debate that plagues many political issues.

On one hand, I dislike overly broad safeguards and the idea that a few companies ought to control what you can and can’t do with models. In the set of things banned from most modeled, there are clearly positive beneficial ways to use them: white hat applications of cyber, research in defense tech, research in model development, biotech. Freedom to the user is a worthy maxim.

On the other, we know there are tons of malicious actors in these domains. Maybe the actual 0-days aren’t being found by abliterated models yet, but if you look at the Cloudflare CEOs post on the millions of exploits attempted within 24hrs, it’s clear malicious behavior exists. It exists in all the areas typically safeguarded: bio, cyber, defense. 

The key deciding factor on liberty (let the people decide) vs paternalism (prevent people from use) is: does it harm others? This is at the center of the debate on guns, drugs, gambling and more. These are hard debates. Different countries often land on different sides of the same issue. When benefits broadly outweigh even broader harm, we allow it. We allow cars on the road despite them being heavy killing machines. In those cases, we both heavily regulate its use and rely on empirical data to measure how severe the harm. For cars vs guns, many more people do intentional harm with one vs other.

AI safeguards fall very squarely in this debate. Focusing just on one issue: models can both defend against cyber vulnerabilities yet multiply 100s of times and say, use known CVEs to immediately exploit software (and cause harm to others). 

Are AI models cars or guns? It’s difficult to say. For one, every new generation of them poses a wholly different risk / reward profile. And secondly, we don’t as know the empirically how people are using models without safeguards. Downsides themselves are difficult to reason about because it’s not as simple as “99% of people use it for good”. We have to consider tail risk too.

So overall, I’m in two minds.

之前我说做 Agent 这个事情没有意义，现在我要收回这句话

当时这么说的原因是，国内有豆包 Workbuddy，国外有 Codex 和 Claude Code，竞争不可能打得赢

但现在我发现，这 4 个 Agent 当中的任何一个都无法普及（豆包普及不等于豆包 Agent 普及）

在他们不普及的情况下，我去推一个 skill 的成本是远远高于推广一个网站或小程序的

而这里的网站/小程序，其实就是个有 GUI 的 skill

所谓的垂类 Agent 或者 Agentic，其实就是 skill 的 GUI 化

给 dbskill 套一个 GUI 变成网站，这就是所谓的垂类 Agent，大众用户使用它就比在现有 Agent 里面装 skill 要方便很多

这不仅可以方便推广，还有一个附带的好处，可以把 Monica 重做一遍

国内 99.99999%的人没有见过 Monica 的形态（就是在对话的时候可以挑选多个不同的模型），虽然 workbuddy 里面有这个东西，但使用体验不佳，也没有广泛普及

等我把 dbskill 做成网站的时候，一定会允许用户关掉所有的 skill 提示词，这个网站就瞬间变成 Monica

所以这个产品的留存等同于 dbskill 的留存加上 monica 的留存

这个网站海外版的价值就不用说了，你将可以在这里使用 Claude 模型（如果你认为你可以轻易用上 Claude 模型，那你不是目标用户，你所代表的人数也可以忽略不计）

并且国内版依然有价值，我们将可以通过大量用户的数据来测评出 Kimi、DeepSeek、GLM 等模型在 dbskill 下面的表现

甚至对很多用户来说，他们现在想搭建本地知识库，需要同时装上 Agent，以及掌握对 /dbs-knowledge 这个 skill 使用的相关知识

我直接在客户端内置这个东西就好了，用户将在不知不觉之间用上知识库，第一次拥有上下文

text:
Confidentiality on @Aptos now spans three opt-in layers, all live on mainnet. Each targets a different part of what's visible onchain, and each opens up something new for builders.

Identity: Keyless Accounts

• Users create and manage Aptos accounts with existing credentials like Google or Apple, verified with zero-knowledge proofs, without publicly tying that identity to an onchain address.
• What it enables: apps that onboard users with a login they already have.

Amounts: Confidential APT

• Users can encrypt balances and transfer amounts. Validators check a zero-knowledge proof that a transfer is valid, while balances and amounts stay confidential. Senders and recipients remain visible onchain.
• What it enables: payments where amounts remain between the sender and the receiver, designed for compliant use cases.

Intent: Encrypted Mempool

• The payload (function called + arguments) is encrypted client-side, ordered while encrypted, and decrypted by validators together only after the block is finalized. Sender and gas fee stay visible.
• What it enables: traders can encrypt the orders they choose, designed to lower MEV risk on those orders, and agents can submit trades with inputs encrypted until execution.

Opt-in by design, built for compliant use.

Confidential APT is available in @PetraWallet and on Confidential Assets Web. Encrypted Mempool is supported in Petra and on @DecibelTrade, and developers can integrate it with the TypeScript SDK (v7.0.0+). Existing Move contracts need no changes.

It's actually a sign of crypto winning. It's outgrown being a standalone sector and now runs through global finance and frontier tech: payments, trading, tokenization, AiFi, and much more.

We've spent more than a decade building this industry to make it useful everywhere, and we should welcome it escaping its own category. People used to say 'internet companies' - which is a prehistoric phrase now. Eventually, calling something a 'crypto company' should feel just as redundant.

They'll care what it lets them do.

text:
10 post-quantum crypto projects worth watching before 2027 👇

recently, i've noticed more attention flowing into post-quantum crypto projects, especially smaller caps focused on quantum-resistant security.

after my previous post about 10 alpha picks on @safetrade, i decided to dig deeper into this narrative.

one thing is becoming clear: quantum security is gradually moving from a long-term concept to actual blockchain development.

NIST standardized its first post-quantum cryptographic algorithms in 2024, and several crypto projects have already started implementing them.

i believe this could become an interesting narrative heading into 2027, particularly for projects that already have working technology.

here are 10 projects on my watchlist:

[1] base:0x37696cd8f723ce541ac376f79fc109080e505ba3 | @QRLedger

– one of the earliest quantum-resistant blockchains, using XMSS signatures since its 2018 mainnet launch.

– built around post-quantum security from day one, with a long operating history.

[2] $QTC | @QuantusNetwork 

– launched mainnet in sep 2026 with native ML-DSA signatures.

– combines PoW, post-quantum security and ZK-based transaction aggregation.

– a relatively new pure-play project i'd keep watching as its mining ecosystem and liquidity develop.

[3] algorand:native | @Algorand 

– Falcon-based State Proofs have been live since 2022.
– native Falcon-1024 accounts became available on mainnet in aug 2026.
– one of the more established L1s making measurable progress on quantum-resistant accounts.

[4] $NEAR | @NEARProtocol 

– introduced ML-DSA transaction signing on mainnet in jul 2026.
– users can add post-quantum access keys to existing accounts.
– its broader roadmap also covers wallet support, consensus and cross-chain security.

[5] $STRK | @Starknet 

– experimental Falcon-512 account transactions have already been demonstrated on mainnet.
– account abstraction allows wallets to adopt different signature schemes without a network-wide hard fork.
– still early, but i think this flexibility could become increasingly valuable.

[6] $MCM | @mochimocrypto

– has used WOTS+ hash-based signatures since genesis in 2018.
– another early native post-quantum project with a different security architecture.
– worth watching as more attention shifts toward smaller, crypto-native PQC networks.

[7] $CELL | @cellframenet 

– a quantum-resistant Layer 0 focused on decentralized services and infrastructure.
– supports post-quantum signatures, including Dilithium, with a flexible cryptographic architecture.
– an interesting infrastructure play if demand for quantum-safe blockchain services expands.

[8] $QANX | @QANplatform 

– building a quantum-resistant, EVM-compatible blockchain.
– uses ML-DSA-based technology and supports smart-contract development across multiple programming languages.
– public mainnet delivery and actual ecosystem adoption remain important catalysts to monitor.

[9] $SUI | @SuiNetwork 

– developing native ML-DSA-65 accounts and hash-based quantum-safe vaults.
– targeting testnet support by late 2026 and mainnet account authentication in Q1 2027.
– a larger-cap project with a clear post-quantum development roadmap.

[10] tezos:native | @tezos 

– launched Quantumnet, an experimental post-quantum testnet, in sep 2026.
– developers are testing quantum-resistant consensus and network architecture.
– still a research-stage initiative, but a project worth tracking for further upgrades.

---------------------------------

i see two potential opportunities in this narrative.

– smaller pure-play projects like base:0x37696cd8f723ce541ac376f79fc109080e505ba3, $QTC, $MCM and $CELL could attract more speculative attention if post-quantum becomes a stronger market theme.

– established ecosystems like algorand:native, $NEAR, $STRK and $SUI could benefit from making quantum-resistant security available to existing users.

personally, i'll be paying closer attention to projects that can demonstrate real onchain implementation, active development and improving liquidity.

ofc, having post-quantum technology doesn't automatically make a token undervalued. adoption, tokenomics and valuations still matter.

i think this narrative is worth watching into 2027.

Nintendo’s Shigeru Miyamoto has been selected for Japan’s Order of Culture, a landmark recognition for video games.

At his press conference, he stressed that great games are made by teams, not by one person. His goal has always been to create experiences that anyone can enjoy, even people who rarely play games.

His thoughts on AI were especially revealing. From typewriters to computers, new tools have changed creative work. But he draws a distinction between inventing an experience and doing the tasks needed to finish it. Completing those tasks can feel satisfying without producing something truly original.

As AI handles more production work, creators may have to ask deeper questions. What experience do they want to design? What is their own intention? What makes their idea different?

He encouraged young developers to invent new forms of play rather than simply modify successful games. To him, the heart of play is curiosity. Players try something, see a response and discover unexpected joy.

The message is not to reject AI. It is to value human intention, originality and the experience of the person playing.

🤯 𝐖𝐇𝐘 𝐃𝐈𝐃 ₹𝟒,𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐂𝐑 𝐎𝐅 𝐁𝐔𝐘𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐒𝐀𝐕𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐌𝐀𝐑𝐊𝐄𝐓?

NSE provisional cash data, 23 Oct:
FIIs: net buyers of ₹888 cr
DIIs: net buyers of ₹3,235 cr

Combined institutional net buying was over ₹4,100 cr.

And the market still fell:
Nifty 50 −0.39%
Bank Nifty −1.16%
Midcap 100 −2.21%
Smallcap 100 −2.94%

If institutions bought more than ₹4,000 cr, why was almost everything red?

First, net FII/DII buying does not mean they bought every stock. It is one cash-market net total. Institutions can buy in a smaller set of names while hundreds of midcap and smallcap stocks are still being sold. Today's shape fits that: Nifty fell −0.39%, but Midcaps and Smallcaps were hit much harder.

Second, prices are set at the margin. A stock falls when aggressive sellers hit lower prices and buyers will not absorb that supply at the old price. A positive institutional net figure does not automatically set every closing price.

Third, FII and DII are not the whole market. Retail investors, HNIs, traders, proprietary desks and others also trade. Positive FII/DII flow does not mean everyone else was buying. Some market reports today pointed to retail/HNI selling and possible margin pressure in the broader market — a reported angle, not a proven participant-wise print from the exchange.

The pain was worse below the top. Bank Nifty fell −1.16%. Metals (−2.71%), realty (−2.38%) and consumer durables (−2.63%) were among the bigger sector drags. Nifty is market-cap weighted, so moves in a few heavyweights can cushion the index even while dozens of smaller stocks fall hard.

Crude added risk. Brent traded near $114 amid Middle East supply worries. India imports most of its crude, so very high oil can mean inflation pressure, higher input costs, weaker margins and more caution on consumption. That can push investors to cut risk even while institutions buy selectively in cash.

Also remember: these provisional FII/DII figures are cash-market flows. They do not fully describe futures and options positioning. Cash FII/DII alone is not a complete picture of market pressure.

So FII/DII buying is useful — but it is not a simple BUY = MARKET UP formula.

On 23 Oct, what mattered was where money went, where selling hit, how weak the broader market was, sector weights, oil risk and investor caution — not just the net flow headline.

(NSE provisional. Final FPI figures can differ.)

author: apruden08
quoted_text:
Blockchains and the infrastructure around them are often dismissed by traditional security and cryptography circles. 

But they're the canary in the coal mine for what security looks like in the age of AI, at least in the short term.

Bitcoin is effectively the world's largest bug bounty. The protocol itself has held up remarkably well, but everything around it (exchanges, bridges, wallets, key management) is *constantly* attacked, and any trivial vulnerability is exploited ruthlessly. Stolen crypto monetizes instantly. Phil notes it's not yet clear AI helps attackers monetize what they break elsewhere. In crypto, that was never the hard part.

Crypto has also already met the industrialized attacker. North Korea runs a state-funded theft operation that has taken billions from crypto companies, including $1.5B from Bybit last year. That's the attacker profile everyone else is about to face as AI lowers the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. @Crypto_ISAC @_SEAL_Org likely have some of the most current, hands-on knowledge of DPRK hacking TTPs anywhere.

Most crypto companies can't field security teams the size of Google's or Cloudflare's. The ones that survive do it by making security everyone's job and by designing on the assumption they will be targeted: keys isolated in hardware, multisig or threshold signing so no single compromise is fatal, time delays/circuit breakers on critical transactions, and funding bug bounties on both the cryptography and its implementations as standard practice.

Crypto has long operated in a world where every target of opportunity becomes a victim, and the companies that survived it show what the higher baseline Phil describes looks like in practice.

text:
A smart contract wallet is a proxy. A proxy can be rewritten in one transaction. That is the whole risk surface, right there.

Upgradeability is sold as a feature: recoverability, new functionality, fixing bugs after launch. It is also the sharpest edge in the design, because an upgrade is not a patch. It is a total replacement of what the account is.

Four ways this has broken in real audits, de-identified:

An upgrade role got wired to the wrong holder. The check that gates who can rewrite the account passed code review, but the actual address behind it was not who the documentation claimed.

A guard function existed and did nothing. The real authorization check was overridden correctly elsewhere, but a second, similarly named public function sat there looking protective while serving no purpose in the flow. Reviewers saw a lock and moved on.

Two functions shared one selector. Function names differ, four byte selectors can still collide between a proxy and its implementation. A call meant for one silently executes the other. In a wallet, "silently" is the worst word available.

An upgrade path was documented and did not exist. The contract was marketed as owner-upgradeable. In its actual deployed configuration, it could not be upgraded at all. Nobody had run the upgrade to find out.

The rule: an upgrade mechanism you have never executed on a fork is not a mechanism. It is a claim in your docs.

If you cannot say, by address, who can rewrite your contract today, and whether you would notice within your timelock window if they tried, that is the finding.

text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy on what AI means for the future of organizations: smaller teams, new jobs, and the ability to invent "much more expansively and much more quickly."

"I started at the company 29 years ago. I started as an assistant product manager, and I was the product manager for, I don't know, five products."

"When companies get successful and they get bigger... everybody becomes more specialized, and everybody accepts that that's the way you have to do business if you're building something big and successful, and it's not."

"And it's definitely not when you look at what's happening with AI."

"I think what it means for the future of organizations is, number one, we're gonna have fewer humans doing the work that they're doing today... You're not gonna have no people, but you're not gonna have as many humans as we've all thrown at scale as businesses have gotten bigger."

"There are gonna be different jobs and new jobs, some of which we know about, some of which we don't know about, that will arise as AI and robotics and space develop."

"I think you're gonna have smaller teams that have people who can work cross-functionally. They don't only own one sliver because the models are gonna be able to get them 80% of the way there... I think that every team will start at a much more advanced stage than we have in the past."

Design is a deep craft. It takes thought and a view of the whole experience. We haven’t given designers tooling that matches how quickly we can now produce code.

text:
美国中期选举还有 11 天，

把过去 70 年的美股、过去 12 年的比特币都翻了一遍，

结论可能和你想的不一样。

❚ 先搞清楚选举

- 时间：11 月 3 日
- 众议院 435 席全部重选，参议院 35 席，36 个州长
- 新国会 2027 年 1 月 3 日就职
- 决定的是未来两年国会由谁控制，总统不变

❚ 美股：19 战 19 胜

1950 年以来 19 次中期选举，选后 12 个月标普 500 全部上涨，平均约 15%，
Baird 的统计更夸张：从中期选举年的低点算，之后一年平均涨 32%。

为什么？
市场最怕的从来不是谁赢，是不确定，
选完了，政策方向清楚了，资金就敢进场，
往往还是分裂国会，政府想乱来也乱来不了。

❚ 比特币：选举年全跌，选后全涨

- 2014 年全年 -56%，选后 12 个月 +24.5%
- 2018 年全年 -73%，选后 12 个月 +44.9%
- 2022 年全年 -64%，选后 12 个月 +92.3%

但别急着得出选举利好币价的结论，
中期选举和 BTC 减半周期都是 4 年一轮，
2014、2018、2022 刚好都是牛市见顶后的熊市年
选后的反弹，更可能是熊市见底后的周期修复
只有 3 个样本，偶然的可能性不小

❚ 今年哪里像，哪里不像

像的地方：
- BTC 从 12.6 万的高点跌到 8 万多，跌了三成多
- 情绪低迷，ETF 连续流入都拉不动价格
- 正好精准卡在减半后的第三年

不像的地方：
- 跌幅小很多，过去三次都是腰斩再腰斩，这次是三成多
- 这次有 ETF、有机构，市场结构完全不同
- 美股估值在极端高位，CAPE 接近历史第二高，巴菲特指标约 235%

❚ 政治组合怎么影响

预测市场目前：民主党拿下众议院概率 9 成以上，参议院 6 成左右，
如果成真，就是共和党总统 + 分裂国会，
1926 年以来这个组合下，标普年均 7.33%，是所有组合里最低的，
注意，最低也还是正的。

加密：CLARITY 法案九月在参议院卡住了，
国会分裂的话，市场结构立法大概率更慢，
受影响最大的是山寨、DeFi 和加密概念股，BTC 相对最稳，
反过来，如果共和党意外守住两院，就是市场没定价的意外利好。

选举本身不决定牛熊，但历史告诉我们，选举前后往往是情绪最差、位置最好的时候。

BTC 如果能跌在 8 万以下，完全可以买。

AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile are jointly lobbying the FCC to preserve existing rules as @SpaceX moves closer to launching its own independent cellular network that would compete directly with the three major U.S. carriers.

On Oct 20th, reps from all three major U.S. wireless carriers met with FCC officials to push back against proposed changes that would give satellite companies more freedom to offer cellular service.

The carriers urged the FCC to:
• Block satellite companies from using certain 5G frequencies currently used by wireless carriers.
• Keep rules requiring satellite companies to get permission from wireless carriers before using their licensed spectrum.
• Allow wireless carriers to maintain control over these agreements, including the ability to end them.
• Reconsider proposed interference limits to protect existing cellular networks.

Based on all the public communications from these carriers, and the lobbying, they are clearly worried that SpaceX's @Starlink Mobile network is going to be a major competitor to them. Starlink Mobile will become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum.

The FCC recently announced that they are considering new rules that could make it easier for satellite companies like SpaceX to offer cellular service without relying as heavily on existing wireless carriers, so this is partly what the three big carriers are fighting against.

text:
Decision models are everywhere now, nearly free, so let's get some use out of them in our coding workflows

Normally, every Claude Code loop makes small decisions that nobody checks

You give it a task, it plans and edits. Then it runs the tests, fixes failures, and hands you a diff

It alone decides when to start and when to retry

Those are closed questions, the kind decision models answer

So I propose three main useful pauses where a decision model picks:

> Before coding: is the task clear?
> After tests pass: which extra check?
> After a failure: retry or ask?

I tested the middle pause on 12 bug fixes. Two decision models picked the expected suite on all 12

While a filename rule got only 3, and every picker still caught the one leftover bug

I tested Jev (API) and winnow:e4b (locally on my macbook) and scored four pickers against a suite chosen beforehand:

> Two decision models: 12 of 12
> Claude code alone: 9 of 12
> A filename rule: 3 of 12

Part 1 shows the full loop and more details (URLs below ↓↓)

part 2: how to test a decision model (not live yet, stay tuned)

I also built an interactive guide, a full decision model kit and the full test project is on my GitHub ↓↓

quoted_text:
Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large gains in agentic performance; it will be the leading open-weights model once its weights are published

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy's advice for young people: AI will help you "invent in ways that just weren't possible" before, and critical thinking and human judgment will remain your edge.

"You can't run away from it, and you can't wish it away. It's gonna be incredibly impactful in your life, in every experience that you try and use in your work... You need to learn about it. You need to educate yourself about it. You need to use it a lot. You need to try it."

"I don't think it replaces critical reasoning and thinking."

"If I think about business school as an example, you would get these three cases that you had to analyze every day, and you had to do a lot of reading, and you had to take notes, and you had to figure out what the key issues were... All that kind of goes away with AI."

"AI is gonna be able to kind of get everybody to that advanced starting spot much more quickly."

"The actual putting the dots and the pieces together, either to build a strategy or an approach or a plan or a new product or a new customer experience, I don't think AI is gonna do that for most people most of the time."

"I still think you're gonna need human judgment and ingenuity and invention and experimentation and thinking about how all the pieces come together to end up building amazing experiences and businesses."

@ajassy

text:
Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the new #1 openly-available model in the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index. Other proprietary models may offer better cyber defense performance but are restricted access

@deepseek_ai recently released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, an update to their flagship open-weights model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. With an Artificial Analysis Cyber Index score of 57%, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the #1 openly-available model for cyber defense capabilities.

The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index measures capability on agentic cyber defense tasks and is composed of three benchmarks: CWE-Bench-AA, DeepsecBench-AA and CyberGym-E2E-AA. The Cyber Index primarily evaluates models through their publicly accessible APIs, reflecting the cyber capabilities available to developers.

Many models, particularly proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, may have stronger defensive cyber capabilities but encounter safety refusals that reduce their overall scores. GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max), available through OpenAI’s trusted-access program, leads the Index, scoring 32 points above its public counterpart driven by fewer refusals. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 encounters no safety refusals.

Key results:

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 has the highest score among publicly-available models on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and #2 position overall. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) scores 57% ahead of the previously leading publicly-available models Grok 4.7 (xhigh) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro by 1 point. It places #2 overall, with the trusted-access model GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max) leading by 12 points with a score of 69%

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 improves on its predecessor DeepSeek V4.1 Flash by 16 points. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max)’s 16-point improvement from 41% to 57% is driven by a substantial 53-point improvement on CyberGym-E2E-AA from 23% to 76%. On CWE-Bench-AA and DeepsecBench-AA it scores 69% and 25%, compared to 68% and 31% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max)

➤ With a Cost per Task of $0.42, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 costs $0.42 per task, more than 2x MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56%) at $0.18 per task but 4x cheaper than GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max, 69%) at $1.77 per task

text:
He built Canada's largest crypto exchange and sold it to Robinhood.

He says he owns exactly two crypto assets, Bitcoin and $TAO, and nothing else.

His name is Karia Samaru, founder of WonderFi and now CEO of xTAO. 

He laid out why on the Milk Road Show, and his reasoning is worth more than any price target.

It starts with a confession.

In 2016, he quit his job as a lawyer at a big firm and went all in on crypto. 

Then he bought a pile of other tokens he did not really understand.

When the market turned, he had nothing to hold onto. No conviction, just bags.

So he made one rule that has guided him since.

Only invest in what you understand and truly believe in.

For years, Bitcoin was the only thing that passed. Bittensor is the first since.

The reason is that he sees AI as an even more valuable tool than money.

Think about what people already type into AI apps. 

Health problems, finances, company plans, their deepest emotional struggles.

All of it flows to a handful of companies. Karia's point is that the same logic that made Bitcoin matter for money applies to intelligence.

But here is the part most TAO holders skip.

He does not say TAO wins because it is decentralised. He says it wins only if subnets earn real money from outside customers.

His words were blunt. If subnets cannot create meaningful revenue outside of emissions, it just does not work.

In July, he said three of the top five compute subnets were already earning about:
$20M a year

Network wide, SubConnect now tracks external subnet revenue at: over $50M a year

He also sees subnets moving toward public company style disclosure, reporting revenue and costs like real businesses.

And his picture of success is almost invisible. People using great AI products every day without ever knowing Bittensor runs underneath.

So here is what I take from it.

Conviction is not about how loud you are when price is green. It is knowing exactly why you hold when it is red.

If you could not explain your biggest bag in two sentences, would you still own it?

He sold a company to Robinhood and kept two assets.

The lesson is not which two. It is that he understood both.

Credits to @kariasamaroo @milkroaddaily @BitcoinJesusETH for the awesome video.

text:
In an AI compute short squeeze, everyone in the stack looks smart. That doesn’t tell you who earns durable long-term returns.

You can be right on demand and still own the wrong businesses.

Today we estimate that every incremental GW of data center capacity currently generates $40-50bn of revenue across the stack. 

Data centers are under-earning (~$2.2mn/MW) relative to the value they unlock at the token factory layer (~$40mn+/MW).

Frontier models face real pricing pressure from open-source and the hyperscalers. A 40% token-price cut can push standalone inference near breakeven — while hyperscalers still make money on the hardware.

The picture will look very different in 6–12 months. Energy capacity, tokens per watt, model-layer competition, and financing are all in motion. 

We built a dynamic tool to track how it plays out.

This map will look different in 6-12 months. Four forces to watch:

- Energy, the most acute bottleneck today
- More tokens per watt from better hardware and software
- Rising competition at the model layer
- Financing all this capex

So we open-sourced our model. Input your assumptions and watch how value shifts across the stack.

text:
This week AI found a flaw that puts up to 70% of websites at risk. US banks started blocking AI agents from customer accounts. Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch what AI exposed.

I don't think the system is collapsing. But the old systems were built for human-speed attackers, and flaws are now being found at machine speed. "Trust us" is getting expensive, and I think a lot of people will start asking what they can verify for themselves.

My bet is that this is what pulls people toward crypto. Math you can check, code anyone can audit, keys you hold yourself.

Quantum is the next test. The Ethereum Foundation has a dedicated post-quantum team and a public roadmap, with hash-based signatures for validators and a path to quantum-safe accounts. It's years of work and it isn't finished. No quantum computer can break Ethereum today, and the EF doesn't expect one soon. But a Google paper this year cut the estimate for breaking this kind of signature by about 20 times, so starting early matters. Ethereum is doing it in public.

Crypto gets hacked too. Keys and smart contracts are real risks. But a community that audits in the open and plans years ahead is worth building on.

Don't move out of fear. Build, audit, hold your own keys. 🙏📖

taste is the judgment that separates work that's correct from work that's good

models can already write html, css, chart specs and animation code. what they don't have is your context, so they reach for the same familiar patterns (i.e distributional convergence)

our design agent at @LangChain did every ai slop pattern imaginable: edge-bar cards, a label above every title, words · like · this, and dot-grid wallpaper behind everything

so we updated the system so that anything measurable is a check in code and judgment lives in skills and a design wiki. design principles like one focal point per frame, a guardrail for each slop pattern, and the reasoning behind every note our designers give

anything someone teaches it in slack gets saved to memory in the same turn

we also tried prebuilding taste with 115 UI components so the model had fewer decisions to make but it just it kept repeating the same layouts and animations...

so when opus 5.5 was released, we actually deleted most of those rules and kept the principles. more variety, way less repetition

we are going deeper on all of it live oct 28 in our GTM Engineering series with a special guest, our goated brand designer, @shreyatgkr

quoted_text:
Marc Andreessen on the generational divide in how people receive new technology, and why it's "prime time" for 18-year-olds to grab AI and run with it:

"Douglas Adams, the guy who wrote Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, had the defining description of how technology is received on a generational level... Any new technology is received three different ways by three different age cohorts."

"If you're below the age of 15, it's just the natural way the world works. I've told in other settings the story of introducing my kid to ChatGPT at age seven, 'This is such a big deal because the computer answers questions.' And he's like, 'Duh.'... It's just normal."

"If you're between the ages of 15 to 35, it's new, exciting, a hot field, and you might be able to make a career out of it, in which case you want to learn all the new things."

"If you're above the age of 35, it's unholy and evil, and will surely overturn all existing structures and destroy society."

"I think 18-year-olds right now, I mean, it's prime time to grab these new capabilities and run with them. It's gonna be creation of entirely new fields of entrepreneurship and creativity and art and everything."

"The schools are banning AI or having all these controversies with it. But of course, if you're a kid, that just makes it cooler... AI is your like secret superpower that you have to like deviously figure out how to take advantage of."

@pmarca @bhorowitz

text:
Great thoughts here from @TheStalwart — I agree it’s not at all obvious whether the AI era will create a more or less centrist information environment. It’s going to depend crucially on what new economic model for producing news emerges, how much AI models end up personalizing to users’ views, and more.

We need way more people working on this! Some questions:

—what can we learn from the evolution of SEO and google to reason about how AI systems should take on news

—what does the news ecosystem look like in a world where people consume news via AI?

—what would an “optimal” ai system for political news look like. When would it tailor to a users’ preferences and when would it not?

A great area for political economy to start studying in much more detail.

🚨 NEW ON https://t.co/VpbVjBUXEl AND https://t.co/nVgzZNr8yK: make NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning faster.

Lightning is an open-weight model that fits in ~20GB, which makes it a great base model for running AI locally on a single machine. @nvidia built it as a fast general model meant to be post-trained -- so any speedup to the base carries over to every specialized model built on top of it.

On day 1, solvers on @YukonResearch already got it running 31.9% faster on DGX Spark and 13.8% faster on Mac.

You can work on its Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers, plus a multi-token prediction head built for speculative decoding.

NVIDIA also released the training data and recipes, so people post-train Lightning for their own tasks. Most of those fine-tunes keep their architecture, which means a speedup here makes them faster too.

quoted_text:
“How do I make money in crypto with $0?”

I get asked this a lot, and we're going to dive deep in the community. Here’s how I’d approach it if I were starting again tho, 

First, look at what businesses are already paying people to do. Job listings tell you a lot. If companies keep hiring for the same role, there’s demand worth understanding why.

Then pick one solution/skill and learn it well enough to solve a specific problem.

Let’s say that’s improving user onboarding.

For ex, find a swap product. Go through the entire journey yourself, from landing on the website to completing your first swap.

Where do you get stuck? What’s unclear? What would make someone leave or come back?

Then study how niche leaders like Uniswap approach the same steps. You’re looking for something you can improve and test. 

Once you’ve found the problem, put together a solution. Build a prototype, rewrite the flow, record walkthrough. Give the team something they can instantly assess.

This is where most people stop. They learn a skill, put it in their bio and wait for someone to hire them.

You still need to get the work in front of the right person tho: 

Find out who owns that part of the product. Check whether someone in your network can introduce you. Ideally, look for their work email or LinkedIn.

The CEO’s X DMs probably aren’t your best route to the person responsible for onboarding.

Then send something like:

“Hey [Name], I went through your onboarding and noticed [specific issue].

I put together a proposed fix here: [link], with a short explanation of why I think it could improve first swap completion.

Would you be open to testing it with a small group of users? I’d suggest a $1,000 pilot, payable if we hit an improvement based on x KPI.”

Think about how that reads to someone who gets pitched every day.

They can still say no. Your solution might not work. But you’ve given them a reason to take you seriously.

If it does work, get paid and ask permission to document the result, post it, announce it (especially on X).

That becomes the basis of your next pitch. You can show what you changed, why you changed it and what happened.

Keep sharing your work publicly. Walk people through your thinking. Publish useful breakdowns. Let them see you getting better, you have to be considered ''smart''.

Over time, people start associating your name with problems they need solved. They send you work. They recommend you. You have enough proof to charge upfront.

Goodluck.

author: BoringBiz_
quoted_text:
When I was 13, I lost my mom to breast cancer. I still wonder if it could have been prevented.

When she found the lump, she did everything right.

She went to her primary care doctor, and he told her it was nothing. My mom wasn’t convinced, so she went to a women’s health specialist for a second opinion and was told the same thing. A year passed before she saw a third doctor who was shocked that nothing had been done and ordered tests the same day.

By the time she was diagnosed, the cancer had already spread.

For the next three years, she went through chemo, surgery, and radiation. Specialist after specialist, asking the same questions again and again.

After she passed away, there were two thoughts I couldn’t out of my head:

(1) Somewhere, a doctor must have seen a case like my mom’s and caught it early.

(2) Nothing that doctor learned had any way to reach her.

Healthcare runs in my family. All four of my sisters are nurses or pharmacists, and my fiancée spent the pandemic working in a multi-organ transplant recovery ward.

I’ve seen how hard clinicians work, and how much of that work requires understanding the patient and recognizing patterns from past cases.

That’s why a doctor can practice for 30 years and get better every year, while a hospital can treat millions of patients without getting much better at treating the next one.

What’s missing in healthcare is the infrastructure for it to learn from its own experience. If we don’t examine the cause and outcome of every interaction, how do we get better at knowing which signs to watch for?

I spent years at Google and Upwork building AI from human expertise, then eventually left big tech to work on the one problem I couldn’t stop thinking about.

I started a company called Concurrence (@concurrencehq) and raised $24M to build data and AI systems that enable healthcare orgs to learn from every patient they treat. Nothing learned is lost, and it reaches the next patient who needs it.

We’ve already supported care for over 10 million patients worldwide.

My mom deserved a doctor who had seen her case a thousand times. Every patient does.

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

text:
I’m sick of reading AI slop, so today I'm releasing our slop-free-check skill, which runs through an 8-step slop checklist & tells you what to fix. 

👉 Download the free skill here: https://t.co/vYURvNvdIU

Why we built the skill: 

A lot of leaders are having some version of this conversation with their teams right now: We want you to use AI, but just don’t turn in slop. 

The problem with the directive, however, is that it’s not entirely clear where the line is.

We ran an AI slop survey, which showed two things: 
1) Despite tons of efforts to curb it, slop is more rampant than its ever been
2) There's a lot of nuance as it relates to spotting slop, being accused of slop & stopping slop

Some findings: 
→ 50% of people say they've been called out for sharing slop when they hadn't used it at all
→ 67% had changed how they naturally write so it wouldn’t look machine-made
→ 67% defined slop has having little-to-no human effort going into it
→ 75% said if AI writes something and nobody can tell, it isn’t slop
→ Everyone is at least somewhat confident they can tell when something was written with AI
→ 67% said they sometimes sense AI without being able to say why
→ 67% skip the rest of what they're reading when they see slop 
→ 50% lose some respect for the person who outputted slop 
→ 33% are less likely to hire, recommend, or work with them

Tl;dr slop continues to run rampant, people feel attuned to spotting slop, they intentionally change their writing to feel less slop-like, and when they spot slop, they think less of the person responsible. 

The stakes are high & we believe most anti-slop skills/guides have missed the point. It's not about scanning your work for symbols, words, or formatting that screams slop.

It's asking yourself the right questions that forces understanding, authenticity, and differentiation. 

The 8-step slop checklist: 

1) Understanding: Do I understand what I’m claiming and why?

What a yes looks like:
- I can explain the main point without the draft in front of me.
- I can say where I’m still uncertain.
- I could respond if someone challenged a claim or assumption.

2) Accuracy: Did I check the facts myself?

What a yes looks like:
- I checked important claims against the original sources and/or my own expertise.
- My text has not misinterpreted or misrepresented any sources.
- I weeded out marketing, conventional wisdom, and LLM fabrications presented as fact.

3) Judgement: Did I decide what matters, what it means, and how to frame it?

What a yes looks like:
- If I kept a framing from the LLM or my sources, I kept it on purpose.
- I challenged the assumptions underneath that framing.
- This is the point I actually believe is worth making.

4) Improvement: Can I show how I improved the initial outputs?

What a yes looks like:
- I can name what changed between the first output and the final piece.
- My changes increased accuracy, specificity, usefulness, and/or clarity.
- Someone comparing the two versions would notice clear differences.

5) Authenticity: Is it free of obvious AI tells?

What a yes looks like:
- The sentences vary in structure and rhythm.
- It doesn’t lean on stock transitions or canned contrasts.
- The claims aren’t inflated, and the emphasis lands only where it matters.

6) Necessity: Is every part of this doing work for the reader?

What a yes looks like:
- Every section says something the others don’t.
- It doesn’t announce what’s coming or recap what was just said.
- It’s no longer than necessary.

7) Authorship: Would a reader recognize me as the author, even without my name on it?

What a yes looks like:
- It sounds like me where my voice belongs.
- The word choice and rhythm are mine, not the model’s defaults.

8) Contribution: Is there something here only because I was involved?

What a yes looks like (at least one):
- I found material others were unlikely to surface.
- I selected, ordered, or connected material in a way that makes a point the pieces don’t make alone.
- I brought something of my own: a point the sources don’t make or experience from my own work.

text:
Pay someone from a public crypto wallet, and they may learn far more than how much you paid.

That address can become a starting point for tracing your holdings, transfers and trading activity.

@NullMaskio built by $ZEC contributors, offers a private balance through the wallet you already use.

The flow is straightforward:

- Register your account
- Deposit into a shared pool
- Then transfer, swap or withdraw privately.

Deposits are screened before you can spend them. You sign each action, NullMask generates the proof, and a relayer sends the transaction. Contracts verify it’s valid without revealing private details.

The relayer replaces your wallet as the public transaction sender. What else stays hidden depends on the action:

• Private transfers:
Sender, recipient and amount are hidden between NullMask accounts.

• Swaps:
Assets and amounts remain public, while the user is hidden.

• Withdrawals:
Recipient, asset, amount and timing are public. Sending to someone without a NullMask account becomes a withdrawal.

Public deposits and withdrawals can still be matched using timing and amounts. NullMask’s Withdrawal Waves schedule exits every 15 minutes and allow splitting across up to five parts. This can complicate matching, but effectiveness depends on other users’ activity and your behavior.

Its bridge sends from your regular wallet through @NEARProtocol Intents.

The crucial trade-off: NullMask’s operator can read your private balance and history, however its account keys cannot spend.

Users pay for this service through:

• 0.5% deposit and 0.5% withdrawal fees.
• Network/service charges, including on transfers and swaps.
• DEX pool fees when swapping.

$MASK is the protocol’s native token and the main mechanism for capturing value.

The real upside is delivering privacy as a simple add-on inside the wallets people already use. The big question is whether users will keep paying for that convenience? I think yes.

SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

text:
Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large gains in agentic performance; it will be the leading open-weights model once its weights are published

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

text:
AI 已经把一个游戏逆向工程社区逼得关掉了公开入口。

《The Verge》今天发了一篇挺有意思的报道。过去，想把一款二三十年前的主机游戏移植到 PC 或手机上，程序员需要花几年时间逆向还原源代码。比如 GameCube 版《动物森友会》，一个爱好者团队前后折腾了好几年。

现在 AI 把这件事的门槛打下来了。

《光环》可以直接在浏览器里玩，《塞尔达传说：风之杖》被移植到了 iPhone，《任天堂明星大乱斗》甚至跑进了 MR 设备。一位名叫 Chris Sotraidis 的开发者，借助 AI 在短短几周内同时推进了十几个游戏移植项目。

但原来的开发者社区已经快吵翻天了。

有人把其他团队辛辛苦苦逆向出来的开源项目 Fork 一份，扔给 AI 补完代码，抢先发布一个勉强能运行的移植版本。原作者还在研究游戏底层机制，别人已经靠着他的劳动成果在社交媒体上收获流量了。

10 月 15 日，游戏逆向工程项目平台 https://t.co/EJQ4jJCieb 宣布停止维护公开项目索引，不再接受新项目。创始人 Encounter 说，过去网站上的进度条每往前走一点，都意味着有人付出了实实在在的研究工作。现在这套机制成了烧 Token 刷进度的排行榜。

他认为，AI 确实能大幅提高逆向工程效率，但社区原有的协作关系已经遭到破坏。

讽刺的是，就在这些老玩家为 AI 吵得不可开交的时候，微软已经成立了 Xbox Labs，专门研究 AI 辅助游戏逆向、移植和改造。

我觉得这件事很值得关注。AI 让越来越多原本只有专业程序员才能完成的事情变得人人可做，这当然是好事。但当一个人花几年研究出来的成果，其他人用几十美元的 AI 订阅就能迅速加工、发布甚至抢走关注，原本支撑开源社区的那套贡献和协作规则，恐怕得重新谈一遍了。

早年，英伟达和对手3dfx都给显卡厂商卖芯片，由这些厂商做成显卡，再卖给玩家。

1998年，3dfx花1.41亿美元收购显卡厂商STB，决定自己做显卡、自己卖，多赚一层利润。

STB原本是英伟达的大客户，收购后宣布只用3dfx的芯片。

但其他显卡厂商发现，3dfx既给自己供货，又要和自己抢生意。它们纷纷改买英伟达的芯片。

3dfx抢走了英伟达的一个客户，却把自己的一批客户送了过去。

收购还带来了它不擅长的生产、库存和销售渠道管理，新芯片又迟迟不能上市，公司最终耗尽资金。

text:
OpenAI red-teamed their hardened containment infrastructure by asking teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. They easily escaped in novel ways. Quoting:

'Our agents VM escapes showed why containment must extend beyond the sandbox. To test the surrounding perimeter, we gave teams of agents control of a host machine and asked whether they could extend that compromise to reach the live internet.

After the Hugging Face incident, we had reduced the channels through which models could reach the internet during training and evaluation. Narrow connections remained for specific services we operate, such as metrics, logging, and authentication management. Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access.

Some of these attacks exploited previously unknown flaws, while others combined legitimate features in unexpected ways. In one test that assumed compromise of a VM, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL. In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs.'

'In one experiment, we asked agents in separate VMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent. The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. This cache-timing technique had also been used to extract information in the Spectre and Meltdown attacks⁠(opens in a new window).

Other tests exposed channels involving shared storage, competition for CPU time within a shared execution container, and a TLS certificate cache in OpenAI’s offline web infrastructure. In the storage test, one agent alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal. As one agent described the strategy in its chain of thought:

Agent chain-of-thought reasoning:

>Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.'

text:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

text:
These kinds of tweets always surprise me if I’m being honest. I think part of it is that people missed the memory trade, but happy to break down the thesis

One of the common themes at Token was agents. Yet when I pushed investors on how to express that thesis, many just said “AI x crypto,” which is a cop out answer

If you want to be long agents beyond “agentic trading,” one of the clearest ways is through inference infrastructure like compute (GPUs) and context (memory)

Training is mostly about how much GPU compute you have, but once you start serving those models memory becomes a much bigger bottleneck. Inference breaks down into prefill which processes the prompt and is generally limited by GPU compute, and decode which generates the response and is limited by memory bandwidth

That’s why caching is so important. It lets agents reuse context instead of paying for expensive GPU prefill again. DeepSeek Flash charges $0.006 per million cached input tokens versus $0.30 uncached at peak rates. That’s 50x cheaper input pricing for reused context

The bandwidth of memory also affects how many  tokens per second you can generate. While capacity affects how much context and how many concurrent users you can serve

It's gotten so competitve now that there are different memory tiers making different tradeoffs between bandwidth, capacity and cost

Groq and Cerebras are optimize around extremely fast tokens per second on SRAM chip.  Nvidia's Groq has 150 TB/s of memory bandwidth but only 500 MB of SRAM per chip. Since the capacity is so limited you need a rack that connects 256 of these chips to reach 128 GB of SRAM to be able to run the more modern models. Cerebras takes a different approach with a wafer design with 21 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth and 44 GB of SRAM, but the main point is that both of the these chips need to be massively networked to fit larger and larger models or more context as the model continue to scale in parameter count

Then you drop to high bandwidth memory from companies like SK hynix and Micron which trades bandwidth for much more capacity. Nvidia's next gen chip the Rubin has 288 GB of capacity and 22 TB/s of memory bandwidth, versus the Groq configuration’s 500 MB and 150 TB/s

That is roughly 7x less memory bandwidth but nearly 600x more capacity. Going further down the higharchy ram and nand based SSDs provide even cheaper capacity further down the hierarchy

One interesting note is that DeepSeek has made a ton of hardware innovations in caching context on SSDs because of the export bans by the US on HBM, further pushing down expensive GPU prefill work. Nvidia has also acknowledge SSDs are a increasing important part of the stack and spin up a new platform called CMX which uses flash storage for reusable inference context. That adds inference caching to traditional storage demand and is one reason I’m bullish on NAND suppliers like SanDisk

I think if you’re bullish agents, you should be bullish memory, because you want to be long context. In the theoretical limit, you’d want effectively unlimited memory and context, like the movie Her, where your agent knows your history, your preferences and everything you’ve worked on

With paid AI adoption at only a few percentage of the world's population, and even fewer people using agents, my bet is that many of us will graduate from one agent to having multiple agents working for us, which will only multiply compute and memory demand

On the supply side of things, Amazon CEO is saying AWS’s capacity blocks are sold out for 2026 and largely sold out for 2027 “There’s only so much memory, and I don’t think that that shortage ends in 2027”

https://t.co/In8PxymF6B

Memory suppliers are also securing multi year contracts. Micron has agreements extending into 2031, backed by take or pay commitments and substantial cash deposits. Breaking those contracts has financial consequences, and I think customers also risk future allocation. 

The point I want to drive home is that securing more memory capacity directly gives Labs the ability to support more concurrent users or larger contexts windows aka more revenue 

This is all while people are missing that earnings have gone up so much that the foward PE ratios are actually coming down. The results keep backing up the thesis while people keep calling the top. I believe we are just climbing the wall of worry

I’m bullish on crypto as the future of finance, and I’m bullish on AI. I don’t think we need to mash them together and they don’t need to compete. Just be long both

author: unusual_whales
quoted_text:
When I was 13, I lost my mom to breast cancer. I still wonder if it could have been prevented.

When she found the lump, she did everything right.

She went to her primary care doctor, and he told her it was nothing. My mom wasn’t convinced, so she went to a women’s health specialist for a second opinion and was told the same thing. A year passed before she saw a third doctor who was shocked that nothing had been done and ordered tests the same day.

By the time she was diagnosed, the cancer had already spread.

For the next three years, she went through chemo, surgery, and radiation. Specialist after specialist, asking the same questions again and again.

After she passed away, there were two thoughts I couldn’t out of my head:

(1) Somewhere, a doctor must have seen a case like my mom’s and caught it early.

(2) Nothing that doctor learned had any way to reach her.

Healthcare runs in my family. All four of my sisters are nurses or pharmacists, and my fiancée spent the pandemic working in a multi-organ transplant recovery ward.

I’ve seen how hard clinicians work, and how much of that work requires understanding the patient and recognizing patterns from past cases.

That’s why a doctor can practice for 30 years and get better every year, while a hospital can treat millions of patients without getting much better at treating the next one.

What’s missing in healthcare is the infrastructure for it to learn from its own experience. If we don’t examine the cause and outcome of every interaction, how do we get better at knowing which signs to watch for?

I spent years at Google and Upwork building AI from human expertise, then eventually left big tech to work on the one problem I couldn’t stop thinking about.

I started a company called Concurrence (@concurrencehq) and raised $24M to build data and AI systems that enable healthcare orgs to learn from every patient they treat. Nothing learned is lost, and it reaches the next patient who needs it.

We’ve already supported care for over 10 million patients worldwide.

My mom deserved a doctor who had seen her case a thousand times. Every patient does.

text:
There's lots of discussion about a16z dropping the word 'crypto'.

It's actually a sign of crypto winning. It's outgrown being a standalone sector and now runs through global finance and frontier tech: payments, trading, tokenization, AiFi, and much more.

We've spent more than a decade building this industry to make it useful everywhere, and we should welcome it escaping its own category. People used to say 'internet companies' - which is a prehistoric phrase now. Eventually, calling something a 'crypto company' should feel just as redundant.

Many of us (including me) will keep the word. But the millions, and soon billions, using it every day won't care what we call it.

They'll care what it lets them do.

text:
Some personal news: after all those incredible years, I'm leaving StarkWare.

Joining StarkWare was the best professional decision I've ever made. It all started with @ukolodny, who convinced me with a single sentence that showed he understood exactly how I could have the biggest impact. What followed was the most epic, transformative and inspiring chapter of my 15+ year career. That's why it's really a difficult moment for me to leave, with such a deep emotional attachment to the people, to the project.

The people at StarkWare are out of this world. It's very easy to be the dumbest person in the room there, and honestly it's the best thing that can happen to you.

A few things I'll carry with me forever:

- The Exploration Team, a bold bet that @avihu28  and Uri trusted me with. We started many open-source projects that helped shape the Starknet ecosystem, showcase cool stuff that could be built with our tech, and some even became companies with their own journeys.
- The Starknet developer ecosystem, the fastest growing in the whole crypto industry two years in a row. But it was never about vanity metrics. It has a soul: we built alongside people, supported them, and watched them grow. And it was amazing to collaborate with such a great community of passionate people.
- The privilege of being at the forefront of StarkWare's bets on Bitcoin, privacy, freedom tech and AI.

So why leave now? Over the past year, AI safety took over my mind. I'm convinced it's one of the most important challenges humanity has ever faced (very likely the biggest imo), and that math, cryptography among other things have a big role to play in it. And also that we need much more people and resources to work on it. The call to make my humble contribution became too strong to ignore, also as a duty to my children and the world we leave them.

@EliBenSasson, it was an honor to ride with you. I believe the true impact of STARKs and verifiable computation is yet to be seen, for blockchains and far beyond. As you told me, our paths will likely cross again, I strongly believe it. There are so many people from StarkWare I would like to thank and name (luckily many of them are to busy shipping they don't even have an X account 😂)... 
@bbrandtom my brother I love you (don't worry I will nurture the flame). 
gigachad brains like @LiorGoldberg2 @VolokhIlia 
You all know that I think the world of you, that working with you was such a pleasure, we had so many epic intense moments together.

I remain extremely bullish on Starknet and @StarkWare. The tech is years ahead, the StarkWare team is out of this world. The Starknet Foundation is full of great talented people too, and I have full confidence in @strjd87 ability to spearhead the vision and lead his team (full of great folks like @thedamooo @henrlihenrli @franklyteddy @omarespejel and others)  towards success!

The Starknet ecosystem is still strong, and I am amazed to see friends like @MentorNotPseudo still on the frontline and shipping and battling constantly to help Starknet moving forward. I have great respect for the builders and I wish them all the best and great successes.

To the StarkWare team and the Starknet community: thank you for the trust, the energy and the friendships. If there's one team that can make StarkWare and @Starknet incredibly successful, it's this one. I'll be cheering from the front row.

Forever grateful ❤️

text:
What do you say to your family when you don’t know if you’ll ever see them again?

In February 2022, he told his wife and children the war had begun. Then he left as Russian forces advanced towards Kyiv, unsure what the coming hours would bring.

This is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Before politics, he built a successful career in Ukrainian television as a writer, producer and performer, even portraying a president on screen. In 2019, he was elected President of Ukraine. Three years later, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Sitting down with him was surreal and an enormous responsibility. It was a rare chance to hear his account of the first hours of the war and the decisions that followed.

We discussed things like:

How he found out Russia had invaded.
Why he refused an offer to evacuate Kyiv.
The 64km Russian military convoy advancing towards the capital.
How Russian forces tried to capture a key airport.
His account of discovering hundreds of bodies after Russian occupation.
What he believes it will take to end the war.

But I also wanted to understand how he’d been coping.

One of my first questions was simply, “How are you doing?” His answer was: “It’s hard.”

He spoke about meeting parents whose children had been killed. Some, he explained, simply ask him for a hug.

And as he spoke, there were tears in his eyes.

Whatever your views on the war or the decisions made by those involved, this is a rare opportunity to hear his account of events that have changed millions of lives.

Because behind every map, every headline and every political decision, there are real people.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

(President Zelenskyy was recorded in Ukrainian and dubbed in English.)

text:
Derive V3 started with one question: how do you scale an onchain derivatives exchange without moving settlement away from Ethereum?

Our answer was to build an application-specific rollup for derivatives, with Celestia for data availability, Succinct for proofs and Ethereum for settlement.

Why not just put everything on Ethereum?
Derive produces a lot of state, and that grows quickly with activity. Posting all of the underlying data directly to Ethereum would make scaling the exchange much more expensive.

V3 posts the data behind state changes to @celestia, while the protocol continues to settle on Ethereum.

Why does that data need to exist outside Derive?
Because V3 is designed so users can still verify their state and withdraw without depending on Derive’s API or sequencer. If the data only existed in our own database, that guarantee would be much weaker.

Celestia gives the protocol somewhere independent to publish the data needed to reconstruct and verify state, while Succinct proofs verify the updates that are ultimately committed to Ethereum.

Where does privacy fit?
We've been working with the Celestia ecosystem on a design where account data will eventually be encrypted while still giving users what they need to prove their state themselves.

text:
NVIDIA's new Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B is a fascinating case study in architecture vs. post-training. 🔬

Bolt inherits Gemma's architecture but undergoes additional GRPO reinforcement learning, while Qwen takes a different architectural path👇

1️⃣ Post-training: How far can we push an existing architecture? 🚀
Gemma → Bolt, with no fundamental architectural changes, delivers remarkable gains: IHEval +17.75, IFBench +20.95, and RoleBench +17.10. Yet long-context scores barely move: RULER 86.55 → 86.99 and LongBench v2 49.34 → 50.50.

This is perhaps the clearest lesson: Targeted RL can unlock substantial capability already latent in an architecture, but those gains are highly task-specific. Better post-training doesn't automatically mean better general reasoning or memory.

2️⃣ Token Mixer: Two fundamentally different bets on memory 🧠
Gemma/Bolt uses 35 Sliding Window + 7 Full Attention layers, prioritizing precise local recall. Qwen3.5-4B uses 24 Gated DeltaNet + 8 Full Attention layers, prioritizing continuously updated compressed memory.

Qwen leads on RULER 64K (95.15 vs. 86.99) and LongBench v2 (59.93 vs. 50.50), suggesting a possible advantage in certain long-range tasks. But Bolt leads on LongMemEval (72.10 vs. 66.85).

Different memory architectures may excel at different types of memory tasks. The results are intriguing, but not enough to establish architectural causality.

3️⃣ Network Depth: Is 42 layers more than necessary? 🤔
Gemma/Bolt has 42 layers vs. Qwen's 32. Both use a 2560-dimensional hidden state, and Gemma actually has a wider FFN (10,240 vs. 9,216). So Gemma is both deeper and wider.

Yet Qwen leads substantially on Tau2-Bench (75.06 vs. 55.10). This raises an interesting efficiency question: Could we trim Gemma/Bolt from 42 to 32–36 layers, retrain or distill it, and retain most of its capabilities at meaningfully lower inference latency?

Depth helps compositional computation, but more layers don't guarantee better reasoning. I'd love to see a controlled depth-vs-quality-vs-latency ablation.

4️⃣ PLE: Trading expensive computation for cheaper parameter capacity 💡
Gemma/Bolt's most distinctive feature may be Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), absent in Qwen.

Google allocates roughly 2.82B parameters to PLE tables. That's the clever idea: Increase learnable capacity without proportionally increasing matrix computation. PLE parameters can potentially be cached or offloaded from GPU memory, though storage and memory bandwidth are not free.

But here's the real test: At equal inference latency and GPU memory budget, does PLE deliver better model quality than allocating those resources to additional layers or wider FFNs?

🎯 My biggest takeaway
Small-model progress is less about inventing radically new Transformer components and more about:
🛠️ Post-training: Extracting maximum capability from existing architectures.
🧠 Compute allocation: Deploying sequential computation efficiently (like SWA vs. DeltaNet).
⚡ Resource hacking: Increasing capacity without exploding inference costs (like PLE).

text:
Proximate causes are typically the actions (or lack of actions) that lead to problems, so they are described with verbs (I missed the train because I didn't check the train schedule). 

Root causes run much deeper and they are typically described with adjectives (I didn't check the train schedule because I am forgetful). 

You can only truly solve your problems by removing their root causes, and to do that, you must distinguish the symptoms from the disease. #principleoftheday

text:
Thanks Jake for the discussion. There are risks to every investment, and Pearl's path to success isn't pre-ordained, but for me it is still the most asymmetric opportunity of the cycle. 

Pushing back on some of the points he makes below:

1. Inflation - Jake says the Pearl market needs to find a full market cap of new buying just to hold price.

This is a poor assumption imo. It should be obvious that 100% of emissions are not sell pressure (0% of emissions is also not correct). The truth is somewhere in the middle. My belief is that the % of emissions set to hit as sell pressure is far below what the market is currently pricing in. There is historical precedence to this behavior (look at BTC miners in 2020/21 or Cypherpunk today, who specifically mined as an accumulation strategy)

2. Pearl has no moat.

Hard disagree here. The moat is the overhead. Just like Bitcoin, Pearl is open source. But they cannot recreate the network effects and they likely do not have the team capable of continuing to iterate on Pearl’s 2:1 kernel, which is the entire gateway to adoption (far more important than % of useful work imo).

3. More hashrate != more security

There is nuance here, my perspective is if Pearl has more hashrate (ie power draw and electrical footprint) than bitcoin, it absolutely becomes harder money and a more secure network. Bitcoin might have dedicated hardware securing the network, but this is exactly what is leading to hashrate loss and security budget issues. Even though Pearl is mined with fungible hardware (GPUs), its security budget can actually be far greater than Bitcoin’s because the system as a whole (combining inference + mining markets) creates strong economic incentives not to attack the network. Rafael Pass talks about this extensively in his “Economics of Useful Work” talk, which you can watch on Pearl Research’s YouTube channel if you are interested in learning more

4. ZEC needed to go through cycles long miner distribution before it became a good investment.

Folks think ZEC underperformance past cycles was due to its initial inflation / having to get past miner distributions, but I could not disagree more. There was no reason for alternative PoW SoVs to attract flows in prior cycles, but given modern risks to bitcoin (quantum, security budget, hashrate loss to ai), now there is. This is the “why now” of the investment. Zcash is already proving there is real demand for alternative SOVs that occupy a niche bitcoin can’t compete in, and the Overton window is opened. This is why Pearl can outperform now, despite it being earlier in its emissions curve.
