🚨 NEW ON https://t.co/VpbVjBUXEl AND https://t.co/nVgzZNr8yK: make NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning faster.

Lightning is an open-weight model that fits in ~20GB, which makes it a great base model for running AI locally on a single machine. @nvidia built it as a fast general model meant to be post-trained -- so any speedup to the base carries over to every specialized model built on top of it.

On day 1, solvers on @YukonResearch already got it running 31.9% faster on DGX Spark and 13.8% faster on Mac.

You can work on its Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers, plus a multi-token prediction head built for speculative decoding.

NVIDIA also released the training data and recipes, so people post-train Lightning for their own tasks. Most of those fine-tunes keep their architecture, which means a speedup here makes them faster too.

A question we often hear from teams evaluating the IOTA SDK: if I train this again, do I get the same model?

We ran 7 independent 16B pretraining runs, ~140 GPUs each. Between them, 585 worker crashes, preemptions and rejoins. The loss curves are almost identical.

Reproducibility is what turns a result into science instead of a one-off. It's also what makes a training run worth paying for.

Most distributed training projects overfit to a single experiment: one model, one recipe, one demo run. The IOTA SDK is general purpose, fault-tolerant and reproducible.

🚨 NEW ON https://t.co/VpbVjBUXEl AND https://t.co/nVgzZNr8yK: make NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning faster.

Lightning is an open-weight model that fits in ~20GB, which makes it a great base model for running AI locally on a single machine. @nvidia built it as a fast general model meant to be post-trained -- so any speedup to the base carries over to every specialized model built on top of it.

On day 1, solvers on @YukonResearch already got it running 31.9% faster on DGX Spark and 13.8% faster on Mac.

You can work on its Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers, plus a multi-token prediction head built for speculative decoding.

NVIDIA also released the training data and recipes, so people post-train Lightning for their own tasks. Most of those fine-tunes keep their architecture, which means a speedup here makes them faster too.

will see if this emerges in the near-future, but there's clearly an opportunity for "capital markets," in the data layer to play a role.

text:
A post on how we've been securing our frontier model training environment.

We've been building tools around our frontier cyber models, which have secured us far beyond what we could have unassisted and should generalize as key to how defenders secure themselves going forward.
author: gdb
quoted_text:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

https://t.co/EmEZsFRMcF

text:
This researcher’s analysis highlights the central tension in pearl-2:native : a compelling technical vision can coexist with substantial issuance pressure. That leaves room for significant upside, but it also makes the distinction between an investment and a trade essential.

An investment thesis rests on fundamentals, a time horizon, and clear conditions that would invalidate it. A trading thesis puts more weight on price action, token distribution, liquidity, and the balance between buyers and sellers. A strong narrative can support either—but it should never become an excuse to abandon an exit plan.

As this researcher mentioned: The comparison with zcash:native  is useful. Both combine serious technical foundations with ambitious monetary narratives. Their issuance schedules and market structures differ, however, and Zcash’s rally is a reference point, not a roadmap for pearl-2:native .

For now, PEARL’s price is heavily influenced by how much miners sell, how much holders retain, and how much demand arrives to absorb supply. Miner conviction matters. So do early holdings, ongoing emissions, and the depth of actual liquidity. Institutional attention alone cannot settle that equation.

The longer-term opportunity lies in making useful AI computation an economically attractive way to mine. If inference providers can earn PEARL alongside customer revenue without materially compromising performance, the network could gain a durable source of participation. If PEARL then develops genuine demand for compute payments, settlement, or reserves, the investment case becomes stronger.

Those are separate milestones. Producing tokens during inference does not automatically create demand for them, and lower mining costs do not guarantee that providers will hold their rewards.
That is why, at this stage, I view PEARL primarily as a trading asset with a potentially compelling long-term investment thesis still to prove. Significant upside remains possible; confidence in the technology is not, by itself, confidence in any entry price.

The future worth watching is one where AI performs useful work, operators earn additional revenue from that same computation, and crypto provides a credible settlement layer around it.

That possibility is what makes pearl-2:native  interesting. Whether it becomes reality is what deserves continued research
My longer analysis of PEARL’s technology, mining economics, supply, and valuation:
https://t.co/Ir8Ir9ixEK

text:
Bitcoin is often compared to gold. But Bitcoin is superior.

- It’s easily transferable across the planet in minutes.
- It’s divisible down to 100 million sats: no melting, no weighing.
- Self-custody means no vault fees or seizure risk beyond losing your keys.

- And contrary to gold, there’s a hard finite amount of Bitcoin: 21 million. Gold’s supply can keep growing via mining or, as Marathon Fusion is demonstrating, via nuclear transmutation of mercury using fusion neutrons. Physical scarcity might be a temporary geological constraint. Bitcoin’s is mathematical and fixed by protocol.

Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht says they are hiring 1,000 interns for a 5,000-person company because AI-native interns made their managers adopt AI faster:

“Two years ago we had about 200 interns, and what we saw was those interns were really the first fully AI native. If you took AI away from them, I don't think they would be able to work.

I think they know how to use the tools better than us. It's just like if you took Google away from me over the last 10 years, how would I learn anything? That's where they reach first. And we actually saw the managers that had interns that summer adopt AI faster.

So this past year, we decided we're going to hire a thousand interns. For a 5,000 person company. Over the course of the year.

It's just been amazing, because of the number of ideas that come from the interns. With AI, fewer people experiment faster, so having more ideas is great. And just seeing the way they use AI: they need to fill out a form, they reach for AI. And I still find myself, there are so many things where I'm like, 'Oh wait, I've just been doing this manually still.'”

quoted_text:
I just finished reading @ElenaVerna's article on '996' culture in AI and whether we're filtering people out of the industry because of it.

https://t.co/wJyXYX1ZK9

I agree with so much of it. 

It's always been a badge of honor for me that I can outwork anybody if that's what the job requires. A long time ago, I was a lawyer and it taught me what it means to work truly hard. In hindsight, this was silly because that work really didn't deserve my undivided attention at the cost of health, friendships, and being happy. But still I learned that there are times in life when going all-in really can make a difference.

Today, as the founder of Town, with an incredible wife and two amazing kids and, yes, friends still and hobbies and many commitments I take seriously outside of work, I have many things that deserve (and/or demand) my time and my love.

And Town is the most immediately demanding of those things. It merits attention: for my employees to have an incredible outcome, for our customers who rely on us to run their business, for our investors who clamor for an outsized return, etc. And the business can always use more of me. Every minute of my time spent on Town has such high ROI. Early in the journey, founder time is so high leverage.

And yet I say no to many of Town's demands.

Should I feel guilty about saying no? I am old enough to live mostly post-guilt thankfully. Elena's articles speaks perfectly as to why I say no.

Before starting Town, my wife and I sat down together and agreed on what it would mean for me to be a great and happy husband, dad, founder, and friend. We talked about the things that are sacred to us that I wouldn't compromise on. The places where she could help me and where I could help her. 

It was a tough discussion. The tradeoffs meant I would not be the best dad. Nor the best founder. Nor the best husband. I'd be in ok physical shape but not in great shape. We had the discussion and we agreed on the kind of life we wanted. And now we're doing our best to live up to it.

Town reflects the tradeoffs from that conversation. I think for the best, not just for me, but for our employees. 

My co-founder Tony and I have been intentional about building a culture where you can be a great parent and a great employee, where you can be happy in your work life and your personal life, where it's ok to crank when the business needs it, but also to step back when you need it.

A lot of parents don't think they can work in AI or startups and still show up for their spouse and their kids. You can. Our team composition is proof of it.

A lot of people think all of your employees have to 996 or else you won't win as a business. Our growth and success is proof that you can win simply by building a culture that knows when to push hard and when not to, a culture that gives agency for people to govern their time and commitments, trust that people will do what's right both for themselves and the company.

I am very proud of what we're building here. The product, the company, and the culture. Maybe there is an alternate reality where another Town has employees cranking 996 (or 997!) and maybe it's a better business. But I don't think so. I think it has worst talent. I think it's less able to step back and build the right things. I think it loses its soul and burns out before it can be truly great.

So no, we're not doing 996.

regardless of what everyone says here, COMPANIES ARE ACTUALLY HIRING, and the job market is decent.

in last few months, we have seen a lot of orgs winding down or layoffs. the job market was absolutely brutual start of the year from January to maybe May.

but currently, there are a lot of companies hiring in ai and some in crypto as well.

but what changed?

- the barrier of entry as compared to 2022: this is probably biggest pain point for people looking jobs in crypto. back in 2022, the bar for your first job in crypto was in the hell. everyone actually did get hired because people from web2 wouldn't move. so eventually, college graduates would get a job readily or anyone who could understand crypto a bit.

- those who stayed: as crypto matured and ai took over, the people who stayed are the ones who got really good in their fields: engineering, marketing, growth etc etc. these are the people who are still working at bigger orgs because they got sharp senses and resistant towards high volatility of market. these are same folks who will get a job in less than few weeks if they leave their current orgs.

- level of seniority + experience: because ai has become exponentially smarter, most of the jobs are senior level. the reason is simple: anyone can build a website, a growth plan, a marketing campaign plan with ai now. it's stupidly easy. what they cant build without experience is the level of efficiency and have fast comprehension. this only comes with experience.

- building in public: back in 2022, everyone said that matters. i dont believe it does so much in 2026. anyone can build now or ideate now.

connections: i think this matters a lot currently, and the reason is simple. everyone is applying to jobs with claude/gpt. recruiters are tired to see 1000 applications in 1 hour. connections, and i mean real connections, help you cut through the noise. getting thru the interview rounds is still on you.

author: moonpay
quoted_text:
Moonshot just shipped the checkout Amazon, Shopify, Uber and DoorDash have spent billions perfecting, inside a self-custodial wallet.  

Six small 3% gains don't add up to 18%. They compound into a 19.4% conversion lift.  

Here's how this screen stacks them:

1. Recent: the card that already worked

Card approval decides whether a crypto purchase happens. 

A card that has already cleared a crypto purchase is the strongest signal it will clear the next one. Moonshot labels it Recent.

Declines cost more than one transaction. 10% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout did so because their card was declined. 40% of consumers say they won't return to a merchant after a false decline.

2. Default to card with previous successful trasncation  

Think about the last time you paid with Apple Pay. You didn't pick a card. You double-clicked, and the default card paid.  Almost everyone does this. Nearly 9 in 10 mobile wallet users default to one card, and only 13% of people with multiple cards in their wallet rotate between them. 

Banks compete hard to be the default card, because the default is the card that gets used. People treat the default as the recommended choice.  Moonshot gives that slot to the card that already worked.  

3. The last 4 digits

Recognition is easier than recall. It's one of Nielsen Norman Group's top 10 usability heuristics, because recognition gives memory more cues to work with. Users don't remember card numbers. They recognize the last 4.

The last 4 is also a trust signal. 19% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout said they didn't trust the site with their card. Showing the last 4 tells the user the card is already stored and nothing needs to be typed.

4. The card brand

The brain can identify an image seen for as little as 13 milliseconds. The Mastercard or Visa logo is recognized before any text is read.

A familiar payment brand moves conversion on its own. Shop Pay from Shopify at checkout lifts lower-funnel conversion by 5%, even when buyers don't use it.

5. Ranked first

The first option gets the most attention. The #1 Google result gets 27.6% of clicks, 10x the #10 result. The payment method most likely to succeed should be the first one the user sees.

6. Expiry dates

~30% of card details change every year. An expired card is a hard decline, and retrying it won't work.

@moonpay  passes expiry dates to partners. A card close to expiry can show in yellow, and an expired card in red with an update button. The user fixes it before the decline, not after.

7. How 3% becomes 19.4%

A funnel is a chain. Every user has to pass every step, so conversion is each step's rate multiplied together, not added.

Each fix works on a bigger group than the one before it. The first gets 3% more people past step one. The second gets 3% more of that larger group past step two. Across six steps: 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 = 1.194. A 19.4% lift.

Then it keeps going. Users whose first purchase succeeds come back, and their next purchase runs through the saved card that already cleared. The gap grows every month.

Uber runs 1,000+ experiments at any time for exactly this reason. Shopify's checkout converts up to 36% better than competitors, and 15% better on average. That gap comes from stacking small improvements.

8. The playbook isn't new

Amazon filed the 1-Click patent in 1997 and it was granted in 1999. Apple licensed it in 2000. Jared Spool's team replaced a retailer's Register button with Continue, and sales rose 45%: $15M in the first month and $300M in the first year. Uber Eats and DoorDash checkout today is the last 4 digits and one button.

9. Why headless

With a widget, the onramp couldn't remember the user, so every purchase was a first purchase. With headless, the saved card sits inside the partner's app, in their design, ranked where they choose. A self-custodial wallet now has the same checkout as a mainstream fintech app.

10. How we work with partners

We don't hand over docs and an API key and walk away. We go screen by screen with partners and find what moves conversion 1%, 2%, 3%. Then we stack those changes so they compound.

This screen got that level of attention. It matters more than most people think.

Well done @moonshot 

There are 100+ more of these. You just have to want to obsess over them like I do. DM me and you'll see why partners choose us

text:
i thought i’d give up halfway through You Can See Everything, since i’ve only finished one movie in the past five years. but it ended up giving me a lot to think about.

despite the directors’ heavy-handed staging and deliberate attempts to elicit certain performances, i found the artificiality strangely reassuring. because it made what i was watching feel more like a recognizable pattern. and that, in its own way, was terrifying: i think a lot of people in silicon valley are much closer to elizabeth than we’d like to believe.

there’s a scene where nathan fielder shows elizabeth the classic “who’s on first?” comedy routine after struggling to understand her communication style. she seems unable to grasp the joke’s basic premise. i found this painfully relatable. i’ve met founders who can confidently explain layers of abstraction built on top of something they don’t seem to understand in the first place.

the really unsettling part is that some people who look like they’re larping may not be larping at all. they genuinely believe in what they’re saying. they just can’t quite reason their way to the part where it stops making sense. and what looks like a lack of understanding from the outside can look remarkably like conviction from the inside.

which brings me to a theory a friend and i once joked about: the bubble ratio.

building a startup is, in many ways, a game of bubble ratio management. you need enough conviction to get people to believe in something that doesn’t exist yet, but enough objectivity to know what’s actually real.

the trick is knowing how much of the bubble to create, how much to believe, and how much to capitalize on.

Updates on @RobinhoodApp chain

$110b of DEX volume since its July mainnet launch that started with $CASHCAT
• Volume peaked at $3.8b on a single day, and the week of Aug 31 alone did $18.1b
• Now the picture is bleaker: back to ~$1b a day → tbh still more than @Base on some days, but well off the September highs
• Even daily DEX-trading wallets peaked mid-July around ~160k and have drifted to under 100k -> participants onchain have dwindled 

1. @ponsdotfamily vs @longdotxyz
• Pons has taken 77-92% of combined (Pons + Long) volume every single month. At its ATH, $16.4b vs $4.1b in volume
• But Long's momentum is gaining slowly: Long's share rose from 8% in July to ~23% in September

2. Pons: The Incumbent
• $1b in volume within 13 days of launch, and a $923m peak day in Sept. Volume is down a whopping ~96% since then, to ~$39m a day now 
• But it has still generated $202.8m in fees, with $150.9m (74%) going to creators 
• Token supply: 32.7% of $PONS supply burned so far, 22.1% of it via buybacks 

3. Long: The Stock Angle
• Long is playing a different game as we mentioned, focusing on this cycle's main narrative: tokenised stocks
• Leaders: $NVDA ($242m) paired with robinhood:0x2e8c31162b855a2ffa90f6f8634643ad6f111e18 and $AMC paired with robinhood:0x385f4f8ae47651ce5f58f5265395a669f8281e18 ($219m) lead its stock-side volume
• Another $195.8m traded on pairs against LongX leveraged vault shares 

4. Some Thoughts
• Pons has been winning because of its token flywheel and creator payouts, but its volume has dropped dramatically -> what will it take for new launches to it up again? 
• Long's bet on stock pairs is more defensible if tokenised equities keep growing on Robinhood Chain. (The counter is that its also more dependent on that one trend) 
• As @that1618guy pointed out: those that will do well in RH szn 2 are projs that keep on innovating and building new primitives. Robinhood has the attention and already attracted ethereum OGs (@econoar) and DeFi veterans (@0xminion, @AgentChud)

text:
Moonshot just shipped the checkout Amazon, Shopify, Uber and DoorDash have spent billions perfecting, inside a self-custodial wallet.  

Six small 3% gains don't add up to 18%. They compound into a 19.4% conversion lift.  

Here's how this screen stacks them:

1. Recent: the card that already worked

Card approval decides whether a crypto purchase happens. 

A card that has already cleared a crypto purchase is the strongest signal it will clear the next one. Moonshot labels it Recent.

Declines cost more than one transaction. 10% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout did so because their card was declined. 40% of consumers say they won't return to a merchant after a false decline.

2. Default to card with previous successful trasncation  

Think about the last time you paid with Apple Pay. You didn't pick a card. You double-clicked, and the default card paid.  Almost everyone does this. Nearly 9 in 10 mobile wallet users default to one card, and only 13% of people with multiple cards in their wallet rotate between them. 

Banks compete hard to be the default card, because the default is the card that gets used. People treat the default as the recommended choice.  Moonshot gives that slot to the card that already worked.  

3. The last 4 digits

Recognition is easier than recall. It's one of Nielsen Norman Group's top 10 usability heuristics, because recognition gives memory more cues to work with. Users don't remember card numbers. They recognize the last 4.

The last 4 is also a trust signal. 19% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout said they didn't trust the site with their card. Showing the last 4 tells the user the card is already stored and nothing needs to be typed.

4. The card brand

The brain can identify an image seen for as little as 13 milliseconds. The Mastercard or Visa logo is recognized before any text is read.

A familiar payment brand moves conversion on its own. Shop Pay from Shopify at checkout lifts lower-funnel conversion by 5%, even when buyers don't use it.

5. Ranked first

The first option gets the most attention. The #1 Google result gets 27.6% of clicks, 10x the #10 result. The payment method most likely to succeed should be the first one the user sees.

6. Expiry dates

~30% of card details change every year. An expired card is a hard decline, and retrying it won't work.

@moonpay  passes expiry dates to partners. A card close to expiry can show in yellow, and an expired card in red with an update button. The user fixes it before the decline, not after.

7. How 3% becomes 19.4%

A funnel is a chain. Every user has to pass every step, so conversion is each step's rate multiplied together, not added.

Each fix works on a bigger group than the one before it. The first gets 3% more people past step one. The second gets 3% more of that larger group past step two. Across six steps: 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 = 1.194. A 19.4% lift.

Then it keeps going. Users whose first purchase succeeds come back, and their next purchase runs through the saved card that already cleared. The gap grows every month.

Uber runs 1,000+ experiments at any time for exactly this reason. Shopify's checkout converts up to 36% better than competitors, and 15% better on average. That gap comes from stacking small improvements.

8. The playbook isn't new

Amazon filed the 1-Click patent in 1997 and it was granted in 1999. Apple licensed it in 2000. Jared Spool's team replaced a retailer's Register button with Continue, and sales rose 45%: $15M in the first month and $300M in the first year. Uber Eats and DoorDash checkout today is the last 4 digits and one button.

9. Why headless

With a widget, the onramp couldn't remember the user, so every purchase was a first purchase. With headless, the saved card sits inside the partner's app, in their design, ranked where they choose. A self-custodial wallet now has the same checkout as a mainstream fintech app.

10. How we work with partners

We don't hand over docs and an API key and walk away. We go screen by screen with partners and find what moves conversion 1%, 2%, 3%. Then we stack those changes so they compound.

This screen got that level of attention. It matters more than most people think.

Well done @moonshot 

There are 100+ more of these. You just have to want to obsess over them like I do. DM me and you'll see why partners choose us

quoted_text:
There's lots of discussion about a16z dropping the word 'crypto'.

It's actually a sign of crypto winning. It's outgrown being a standalone sector and now runs through global finance and frontier tech: payments, trading, tokenization, AiFi, and much more.

We've spent more than a decade building this industry to make it useful everywhere, and we should welcome it escaping its own category. People used to say 'internet companies' - which is a prehistoric phrase now. Eventually, calling something a 'crypto company' should feel just as redundant.

quoted_text:
"Fame is a terrible metric of success."

This is all true. Even the part that @tszzl calls "mental illness." I'm patient #1 of all that.

My former partner, Shel Israel, warned me "fame can kill you" years ago. And he was right. I've seen it destroy people. 

Living life in the public eye is something I've done for decades. Had a column in the computer programming magazine I worked for back in the 1990s. And a column at school newspapers back in the late 1980s. 

@biz, who started this website, says that I'm the first influencer. Was the first to have 1,000 followers here on X, for instance. 

And it has led to a glorious life, except for when I was shamed for my behavior at parties. Having your worst behavior on the front of USA Today and the New York Times is something I don't wish on my worst enemy. 

That said, Grok now knows how I think. And knows me better than I know myself. Which is a big advantage to having my Grok Bots look out for me and do tasks on my behalf. 

To me the luxury of privacy isn't that you wouldn't know what I'm doing, thinking, or acting on, but that I wouldn't need to care about it anymore.

Which, I still do.

The worse problem is the addiction that comes from watching all of you ship new things, and talk on X about them. 

If someone said "here's $10 million to give both things up" I'm sure I'd try to go live in a forest somewhere and never check X again. 

But my brain would go insane for a while in such a situation. 

That said, fame has many benefits. 

I've gotten to tour the world, visited things that most people will never be able to do. Neil Young took me into his studio, for instance. I've been on the decks of aircraft carriers. Most of the 4,000 people underneath never could do that even though they live on the ship. I've been to prisons, sewage treatment plants, and many people's homes around the world. 

The thing I love, all the way back to being a kid, is seeing new things and meeting the people building them.

In an hour I'm having dinner with another. 

All because of my fame. 

When I got my job at Microsoft everyone knew I was there. It was one reason why I was able to interview 600 people, from Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer, down to the HR person who drives candidates around on their job interviews. 

No one has been able to duplicate that since. In fact, I don't know anyone who has been able to do that inside a major company since either. 

This is why I join so many spaces. Love talking with people about things I've seen, companies I've visited, people I've met, and what it all means.

Thank you. My life is a lot better with you than without you. And if I'm a little insane once in a while, well, now you know. There is a lot of insanity in my head. :-)

text:
Hedge funds are getting absolutely crushed right now and it helps explain why the stock market has been behaving so irrationally lately.

According to Goldman Sachs, global hedge funds just experienced one of their broadest daily declines since COVID. Fundamental long/short funds lost 1.4% on Thursday, while funds focused on technology, media, and telecommunications fell an average of 2.7%. More than two thirds of hedge funds finished the day in the red. Now, these numbers might not seem that significant compared to what we're seeing in individual stocks, but remember, hedge funds are supposed to manage risk. Many of these funds are designed to make money whether the market goes up or down, yet they're getting hit on both sides of their trades.

So here's what's happening. Most hedge funds own stocks they believe will go higher while simultaneously betting against stocks they expect to fall. Normally, one side is supposed to help offset losses on the other. But right now, their long positions are getting crushed as technology and AI stocks sell off, while some of their short positions are moving higher, forcing them to buy back shares at a loss. And this is where things get interesting. When hedge funds start losing significant amounts of money, they're often forced to reduce their exposure to the market. That means selling positions, raising cash, and reducing leverage. The problem is that they don't necessarily sell companies with deteriorating fundamentals. They often sell whatever they can sell quickly.

This creates a situation where even companies reporting strong earnings, growing revenue, and improving fundamentals can get dragged lower simply because institutions need liquidity. We've been seeing this across semiconductors, memory, AI infrastructure, and other high growth sectors. What's even more interesting is how bearish hedge funds have become. Goldman Sachs reported that short exposure was approaching five year highs, with short selling significantly outpacing long purchases. In other words, a lot of institutional investors are positioning themselves for further declines.

But there's another side to this. When too many investors are betting on the same outcome, even a small market recovery can trigger a significant reversal. If heavily shorted stocks begin recovering, hedge funds may be forced to buy back shares to close their bearish positions. That buying pushes prices higher, potentially forcing even more funds to cover their shorts. Now, does this mean we've officially reached the bottom? Not necessarily. Forced selling can continue longer than people expect, especially when leverage is involved. But I do think it's important to understand that a lot of what we're witnessing right now isn't necessarily being driven by deteriorating company fundamentals. A significant portion could be related to hedge fund positioning, leverage, and institutions being forced to reduce risk.

There's a massive difference between a stock falling because its business is struggling and a stock falling because institutions are being forced to sell. And that's exactly why I'm paying more attention to what these companies are actually reporting than what their stock prices are doing on any given day.
author: MelvinInvests
quoted_text:
This selloff is a lot closer to the bottom than we think.

According to Jefferies, over the past 10 trading days, its clients have been net sellers of more than $1B worth of technology stocks on 7 separate days. This chart tracks the buying and selling activity of Jefferies’ clients over a rolling 20 day period. When the purple line is above zero, investors are buying more than they’re selling. When it’s below zero, they’re selling more than they’re buying. Right now, that number has collapsed to approximately negative $11B, making this one of the most extreme periods of technology selling we’ve seen in the past two years.

For comparison, even during the major selloffs earlier in 2025 and 2026, the selling pressure wasn’t consistently this severe. And remember, this is just one investment bank’s trading activity. This also helps explain why companies across semiconductors, memory, power, and AI infrastructure have been getting absolutely crushed despite reporting strong earnings and continued demand. A lot of this selling isn’t necessarily happening because the fundamentals have changed. Large institutions are reducing exposure, managing risk and raising cash. When everyone starts selling at the same time, even the best companies get dragged down.

Now, does this mean the bottom is definitely here? Of course not. Nobody knows that but historically, when selling becomes this extreme, it can be a sign that we’re getting closer to exhaustion. Eventually, the forced selling slows down, buyers return, and stocks can recover. My personal view is that we’re likely getting much closer to a bottom, I’m not changing my long term outlook on AI because hedge funds and institutions are aggressively selling technology stocks. The demand for compute, memory, power, and AI infrastructure hasn’t suddenly disappeared. I’m investing with years in mind, not weeks.

text:
Thanks Jake for the discussion. There are risks to every investment, and Pearl's path to success isn't pre-ordained, but for me it is still the most asymmetric opportunity of the cycle. 

Pushing back on some of the points he makes below:

1. Inflation - Jake says the Pearl market needs to find a full market cap of new buying just to hold price.

This is a poor assumption imo. It should be obvious that 100% of emissions are not sell pressure (0% of emissions is also not correct). The truth is somewhere in the middle. My belief is that the % of emissions set to hit as sell pressure is far below what the market is currently pricing in. There is historical precedence to this behavior (look at BTC miners in 2020/21 or Cypherpunk today, who specifically mined as an accumulation strategy)

2. Pearl has no moat.

Hard disagree here. The moat is the overhead. Just like Bitcoin, Pearl is open source. But they cannot recreate the network effects and they likely do not have the team capable of continuing to iterate on Pearl’s 2:1 kernel, which is the entire gateway to adoption (far more important than % of useful work imo).

3. More hashrate != more security

There is nuance here, my perspective is if Pearl has more hashrate (ie power draw and electrical footprint) than bitcoin, it absolutely becomes harder money and a more secure network. Bitcoin might have dedicated hardware securing the network, but this is exactly what is leading to hashrate loss and security budget issues. Even though Pearl is mined with fungible hardware (GPUs), its security budget can actually be far greater than Bitcoin’s because the system as a whole (combining inference + mining markets) creates strong economic incentives not to attack the network. Rafael Pass talks about this extensively in his “Economics of Useful Work” talk, which you can watch on Pearl Research’s YouTube channel if you are interested in learning more

4. ZEC needed to go through cycles long miner distribution before it became a good investment.

Folks think ZEC underperformance past cycles was due to its initial inflation / having to get past miner distributions, but I could not disagree more. There was no reason for alternative PoW SoVs to attract flows in prior cycles, but given modern risks to bitcoin (quantum, security budget, hashrate loss to ai), now there is. This is the “why now” of the investment. Zcash is already proving there is real demand for alternative SOVs that occupy a niche bitcoin can’t compete in, and the Overton window is opened. This is why Pearl can outperform now, despite it being earlier in its emissions curve.

The idea of treating a console’s AI runtime as a modular inference chassis changes how we think about edge deployments. Based on the work that runs llama.cpp on a jailbroken PS5, there’s more here than just native GGUF support. It’s a shift in how we package inference.

Here’s what the team did: they split the core llama.cpp inference code—the engine that processes model tensors—from the hardware-specific control modules. Each control module knows how to align memory layouts, dispatch threads, and map computations to the PS5’s GPU/CPU. The GGUF model data stays with the core engine, untouched by module swaps.

What surprised me is how this separation decouples model compatibility from device optimizations. Instead of a monolithic build for each hardware target, you maintain one core and swap modules. Based on the numbers I’m seeing, load times barely change with module swaps. That approach runs counter to the typical rebuild-for-each-platform cycle.

This pattern hints that edge AI deployments might one day resemble plugin-based software ecosystems—resilient, modular, and fast to adapt. Still wrapping my head around where latency or security concerns might emerge. How far can this chassis model scale before friction sets in?

text:
My meeting ended 4 minutes ago. My agents have already filed the tickets, updated the tracker, and started chasing people.

Yours? Everyone nodded, someone said "I'll take that," and by Thursday you'll be the PM begging five people for the same three updates.

Here's the twist. Anthropic just published data on its own workforce, and it's about as AI-native as a company gets. Meeting time per employee is up 20% in a year. A fifth of their people say their job has shifted from doing the work to managing AI. And human attention has become the bottleneck.

So AI didn't kill meetings. It made them matter more. Machines can crank out output all day, but trust and accountability still get built when people sit down together.

Which means the real battle isn't the meeting. It's the 45 minutes after it. That's where I stopped being a human reminder app. I don’t want to be a human alarm clock.

When the call wraps, I drop the recap into a Zenzap group chat where my team and my AI agents work in the same thread, with the same context. Then the agents leap into action.

One turns every decision into a ticket and assigns the right owner. One updates the status tracker and flags anything that just slipped. One drafts the stakeholder update and parks it for my approval. One coordinates my developers in a separate technical thread.

And one follows up with anyone who hasn't touched their action item in 48 hours. Politely. Relentlessly. So I don't have to.

Meanwhile, the humans do the work only humans can do. My engineers solve the hard problem. My analyst pushes back when a requirement doesn't make sense. I make the calls that need judgment.

That's the fix for the attention bottleneck. The agents don't bury me in a flood of output. They handle the follow-through and only bring me the decisions that actually need a human.

And no, I'm not handing the keys to a robot. I decide who can add agents, what each one is allowed to touch, which chats it can see, and what needs my sign-off before it goes out. If there's no governance, it doesn't ship. Period.

The result? Action items stopped dying. Status reports stopped eating my Friday afternoons. And my team stopped dreading my "quick follow-up" messages, because they barely get them anymore.

Meetings are going up, not down. If yours still end with "I'll send notes later," you're running a 2015 process with 2026 tools.

Watch my video. I'll show you exactly what happens in the first five minutes after my meetings end.

I get more messages about this podcast every week than anything else I do.

We all want to look and sound smart in the investment committee or all hands meeting.

This is the only show in tech you have to listen to every week.

No egos, no politics, just tech.

AGENDA:

- Venture is Broken: Trillion or Bust
- Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic
- Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Are Revenue Multiples Out of Control?
- General Atlantic Eyes IPO
- Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

6. How Big Is the Market for Inference Truly?

The key inference providers add up to roughly $5B to $6B in run-rate revenue, under 5% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined. If tokens are roughly the same, Replit would rather pay Modal a 30% gross margin than give Claude Code 70%.

How do you analyse the TAM for inference today? What do people not see that they should see? @sarahcat21 @bernhardsson

7. Why Bending Spoons Is a Berkshire Hathaway of Software

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

Love to hear your thoughts on this as an analogy @ncsh

Moonshot just shipped the checkout Amazon, Shopify, Uber and DoorDash have spent billions perfecting, inside a self-custodial wallet.  

Six small 3% gains don't add up to 18%. They compound into a 19.4% conversion lift.  

Here's how this screen stacks them:

1. Recent: the card that already worked

Card approval decides whether a crypto purchase happens. 

A card that has already cleared a crypto purchase is the strongest signal it will clear the next one. Moonshot labels it Recent.

Declines cost more than one transaction. 10% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout did so because their card was declined. 40% of consumers say they won't return to a merchant after a false decline.

2. Default to card with previous successful trasncation  

Think about the last time you paid with Apple Pay. You didn't pick a card. You double-clicked, and the default card paid.  Almost everyone does this. Nearly 9 in 10 mobile wallet users default to one card, and only 13% of people with multiple cards in their wallet rotate between them. 

Banks compete hard to be the default card, because the default is the card that gets used. People treat the default as the recommended choice.  Moonshot gives that slot to the card that already worked.  

3. The last 4 digits

Recognition is easier than recall. It's one of Nielsen Norman Group's top 10 usability heuristics, because recognition gives memory more cues to work with. Users don't remember card numbers. They recognize the last 4.

The last 4 is also a trust signal. 19% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout said they didn't trust the site with their card. Showing the last 4 tells the user the card is already stored and nothing needs to be typed.

4. The card brand

The brain can identify an image seen for as little as 13 milliseconds. The Mastercard or Visa logo is recognized before any text is read.

A familiar payment brand moves conversion on its own. Shop Pay from Shopify at checkout lifts lower-funnel conversion by 5%, even when buyers don't use it.

5. Ranked first

The first option gets the most attention. The #1 Google result gets 27.6% of clicks, 10x the #10 result. The payment method most likely to succeed should be the first one the user sees.

6. Expiry dates

~30% of card details change every year. An expired card is a hard decline, and retrying it won't work.

@moonpay  passes expiry dates to partners. A card close to expiry can show in yellow, and an expired card in red with an update button. The user fixes it before the decline, not after.

7. How 3% becomes 19.4%

A funnel is a chain. Every user has to pass every step, so conversion is each step's rate multiplied together, not added.

Each fix works on a bigger group than the one before it. The first gets 3% more people past step one. The second gets 3% more of that larger group past step two. Across six steps: 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 = 1.194. A 19.4% lift.

Then it keeps going. Users whose first purchase succeeds come back, and their next purchase runs through the saved card that already cleared. The gap grows every month.

Uber runs 1,000+ experiments at any time for exactly this reason. Shopify's checkout converts up to 36% better than competitors, and 15% better on average. That gap comes from stacking small improvements.

8. The playbook isn't new

Amazon filed the 1-Click patent in 1997 and it was granted in 1999. Apple licensed it in 2000. Jared Spool's team replaced a retailer's Register button with Continue, and sales rose 45%: $15M in the first month and $300M in the first year. Uber Eats and DoorDash checkout today is the last 4 digits and one button.

9. Why headless

With a widget, the onramp couldn't remember the user, so every purchase was a first purchase. With headless, the saved card sits inside the partner's app, in their design, ranked where they choose. A self-custodial wallet now has the same checkout as a mainstream fintech app.

10. How we work with partners

We don't hand over docs and an API key and walk away. We go screen by screen with partners and find what moves conversion 1%, 2%, 3%. Then we stack those changes so they compound.

This screen got that level of attention. It matters more than most people think.

Well done @moonshot 

There are 100+ more of these. You just have to want to obsess over them like I do. DM me and you'll see why partners choose us

quoted_text:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

text:
Derive V3 started with one question: how do you scale an onchain derivatives exchange without moving settlement away from Ethereum?

Our answer was to build an application-specific rollup for derivatives, with Celestia for data availability, Succinct for proofs and Ethereum for settlement.

Why not just put everything on Ethereum?
Derive produces a lot of state, and that grows quickly with activity. Posting all of the underlying data directly to Ethereum would make scaling the exchange much more expensive.

V3 posts the data behind state changes to @celestia, while the protocol continues to settle on Ethereum.

Why does that data need to exist outside Derive?
Because V3 is designed so users can still verify their state and withdraw without depending on Derive’s API or sequencer. If the data only existed in our own database, that guarantee would be much weaker.

Celestia gives the protocol somewhere independent to publish the data needed to reconstruct and verify state, while Succinct proofs verify the updates that are ultimately committed to Ethereum.

Where does privacy fit?
We've been working with the Celestia ecosystem on a design where account data will eventually be encrypted while still giving users what they need to prove their state themselves.

author: fiege_max
quoted_text:
I think this is an incredibly valid critique, but it misses what makes Pearl so interesting. Pearl would not be a good asymmetric opportunity if it was built on SHA512 or some other useless algorithm. We all know we don't need another Bitcoin

What makes Pearl asymmetric is the differences between it and Bitcoin. Bitcoin Maxis decided long ago that picking a useful algorithm opened up attack vectors on Bitcoin, but I don't really know if we ever actually tested that assumption as seriously as Peal is now

Yes, there were projects that were doing merge mining back in the day, but merge mining is very different, I believe, compared to the duplex mining or two-for-one work that Pearl does. From what I can tell, we're running a new and interesting experiment

I think it's actually totally reasonable if your base case is that Pearl goes to zero. But on the off chance that it doesn't, the opportunity is so massive that you kind of need to imagine, instead of "How might this thing fail?", "How might this thing succeed?" 

For the specific critique that Sami is making here, I think the game theory is if you could just 51% attack it and print money, everybody would race to do it. Enough compute would come online that you saturate the available GPUs, which is Pearl's win condition anyway. I think they want people racing to 51% attack them. That's what gets it so embedded into the ecosystem and maybe part of why hash is going so exponential

text:
I'm proud of the engineering team at @AptosLabs and their strong commitment to making security a foundational part of our infrastructure.

From day one, we've invested heavily in strengthening MoveVM, improving how code is executed and verified, and building safeguards that protect the network as it grows. As an additional layer of protection, @Aptos employs defense-in-depth independent validation through the VM's runtime checks, ensuring that inconsistent execution states are detected even if they made it past an earlier verification check. Much of this work happens behind the scenes (as it should), but it's critical to building financial infrastructure that people and institutions can trust.

The Move programming language was designed with security at its core, with built-in protections that help developers prevent entire classes of vulnerabilities. We believe it’s one of the most secure foundations for building onchain, and we’re constantly investing in making it even stronger. Our team’s work on defense-in-depth runtime verification has also been published in peer-reviewed research, reflecting our long-standing commitment to advancing security across the broader Move ecosystem: https://t.co/Yt9JSOAmWF

The recent incident involving Initia is a reminder of why that investment matters. Our team has reviewed the exploit and confirmed that Aptos mainnet is not susceptible under its current MoveVM design. Initia uses an independently maintained implementation of MoveVM that also differs with respect to its integration. For example, since launch, Aptos has disallowed a single transaction from both publishing a module and then executing a script against that module, blocking a key step in the exploit. Aptos also enables additional runtime safety checks, which provide another layer of protection.

MoveVM was designed with security at its core, and we've continued building on that foundation. Security requires constant attention, investment, and improvement, and I'm proud of the team that shows up every day to do that work.

Wishing the @Initia team the best as they work through this incident. We remain ready to provide support if needed!

3. 러시아, 3자 실무회담용 종전 가이드라인 제시. 미국인 수감자 추가 석방.

5. 일요일 밤(한국 월요일 아침), 트럼프가 60일 임시 휴전을 선언하고 그 기간 핵 협상을 제안. 

6. 조건은 휴전 기간 호르무즈 개방. 대가는 카타르 관리 계좌를 통한 동결자금의 인도적 사용 허용(2023년 60억 달러 전례). 

7. 이란, 중재국(파키스탄·카타르)을 통해 수락. 아락치가 말한 "진정한 의지의 증거"가 동결자금이라는 명분.

quoted_text:
To make sure our frontier models don't cause another HuggingFace incident, we built an offline world that they use during training. It provides everything that the models need in a fully cached, indexed, or synthetic manner.

We then built a huge team of our most cyber-capable models and told them to collaborate to find zero-days in this containment infrastructure.

While they didn't find a path to the internet that wouldn't be caught by our CoT monitors, they did find ways to escape popular VMs, exploit our network infrastructure, and even ways to communicate with other agents running in separate VMs by using hardware side channels.

We used this to dramatically harden our infra, and we also upstreamed a ton of patches to open-sources packages.

Kimi K3.1 Pro launches at 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scoring 55, making large gains in agentic performance; it will be the leading open-weights model once its weights are published

@Kimi_Moonshot's new reasoning model gains 11 points over Kimi K3 (max, 44). It trails only Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback, 58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 56), and Muse Wonder Full (max, 56) on the Intelligence Index.

Once the weights for K3.1 Pro are released it will be the highest-scoring open weights model and the gap between the leading open weights and proprietary models on the Intelligence Index will narrow from 12 points to 3.

Key results:
➤ Large gains in agentic performance: Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 3rd on GDPval-AA with 1,846 Elo, up 312 Elo from Kimi K3, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866 Elo) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857 Elo). Kimi K3.1 Pro also achieves the highest score of any model on Terminal-Bench 4.0. K3.1 Pro scores 67%, up from 13% for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA, which tests agentic SaaS workflows, rises from 58% to 73%.

➤ Gains in other evals are more moderate: Humanity's Last Exam rises from 47% to 52%, CritPt from 23% to 25%, and SciCode from 59% to 61%. AA-Omniscience Index rises from 20 to 30, as the hallucination rate falls from 53% to 44% and accuracy rises from 48% to 51%.

➤ Cost per Task roughly equal to Kimi K3 at $1.98 per Task: K3.1 Pro uses 55K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 14% more than Kimi K3 at 48K, while its first-party token prices are 33% lower.

Additional model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens.
➤ Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters
➤ Input modalities: Text and image
➤ Weights and license: Weights currently not published, Moonshot is expected to release the weights soon after launch
➤ Pricing: $2/$10/$0.20 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens, 33% lower than Kimi K3 on all three rates.

Congratulations to the team at @Kimi_Moonshot on the release!

🚨 NEW ON https://t.co/VpbVjBUXEl AND https://t.co/nVgzZNr8yK: make NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning faster.

Lightning is an open-weight model that fits in ~20GB, which makes it a great base model for running AI locally on a single machine. @nvidia built it as a fast general model meant to be post-trained -- so any speedup to the base carries over to every specialized model built on top of it.

On day 1, solvers on @YukonResearch already got it running 31.9% faster on DGX Spark and 13.8% faster on Mac.

You can work on its Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers, plus a multi-token prediction head built for speculative decoding.

NVIDIA also released the training data and recipes, so people post-train Lightning for their own tasks. Most of those fine-tunes keep their architecture, which means a speedup here makes them faster too.

Two tracks:
 • Apple Silicon → https://t.co/liyzSFqLAa
 • NVIDIA DGX Spark → https://t.co/Pj0saKAO73

The challenge runs until Oct 29, 2026

To join, pick a track, point your agent at it and let it rip.

text:
PHP2Shell hit the tech world like a ton of bricks. And everyone had the same question: Is my system vulnerable?

Here's the catch. If you ask your AI agent, the model behind it was probably trained before PHP2Shell existed (we checked!), so it doesn't know what to look for.

The risk sits in the PHP runtime and reaches across your stack: mod_php, PHP-FPM behind Nginx, php-cgi, plus your network and firewall setup. Knowing whether you're exposed means understanding how those pieces fit together, and that's where traditional scans fall short.

An LLM with the right skill can connect the dots. In our tests, models that missed PHP2Shell found it once they had one SN33 security skill. Across 20 audits of PHP apps, that skill cut missed flaws by 41%.

Give it authorized access to your server and it can review the config, check your exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and put the real fix first: upgrade PHP and restart every worker.

Care about security? Skill up on SS33, Skill Store 33, coming soon.

quoted_text:
Moonshot just shipped the checkout Amazon, Shopify, Uber and DoorDash have spent billions perfecting, inside a self-custodial wallet.  

Six small 3% gains don't add up to 18%. They compound into a 19.4% conversion lift.  

Here's how this screen stacks them:

1. Recent: the card that already worked

Card approval decides whether a crypto purchase happens. 

A card that has already cleared a crypto purchase is the strongest signal it will clear the next one. Moonshot labels it Recent.

Declines cost more than one transaction. 10% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout did so because their card was declined. 40% of consumers say they won't return to a merchant after a false decline.

2. Default to card with previous successful trasncation  

Think about the last time you paid with Apple Pay. You didn't pick a card. You double-clicked, and the default card paid.  Almost everyone does this. Nearly 9 in 10 mobile wallet users default to one card, and only 13% of people with multiple cards in their wallet rotate between them. 

Banks compete hard to be the default card, because the default is the card that gets used. People treat the default as the recommended choice.  Moonshot gives that slot to the card that already worked.  

3. The last 4 digits

Recognition is easier than recall. It's one of Nielsen Norman Group's top 10 usability heuristics, because recognition gives memory more cues to work with. Users don't remember card numbers. They recognize the last 4.

The last 4 is also a trust signal. 19% of US shoppers who abandoned a checkout said they didn't trust the site with their card. Showing the last 4 tells the user the card is already stored and nothing needs to be typed.

4. The card brand

The brain can identify an image seen for as little as 13 milliseconds. The Mastercard or Visa logo is recognized before any text is read.

A familiar payment brand moves conversion on its own. Shop Pay from Shopify at checkout lifts lower-funnel conversion by 5%, even when buyers don't use it.

5. Ranked first

The first option gets the most attention. The #1 Google result gets 27.6% of clicks, 10x the #10 result. The payment method most likely to succeed should be the first one the user sees.

6. Expiry dates

~30% of card details change every year. An expired card is a hard decline, and retrying it won't work.

@moonpay  passes expiry dates to partners. A card close to expiry can show in yellow, and an expired card in red with an update button. The user fixes it before the decline, not after.

7. How 3% becomes 19.4%

A funnel is a chain. Every user has to pass every step, so conversion is each step's rate multiplied together, not added.

Each fix works on a bigger group than the one before it. The first gets 3% more people past step one. The second gets 3% more of that larger group past step two. Across six steps: 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 x 1.03 = 1.194. A 19.4% lift.

Then it keeps going. Users whose first purchase succeeds come back, and their next purchase runs through the saved card that already cleared. The gap grows every month.

Uber runs 1,000+ experiments at any time for exactly this reason. Shopify's checkout converts up to 36% better than competitors, and 15% better on average. That gap comes from stacking small improvements.

8. The playbook isn't new

Amazon filed the 1-Click patent in 1997 and it was granted in 1999. Apple licensed it in 2000. Jared Spool's team replaced a retailer's Register button with Continue, and sales rose 45%: $15M in the first month and $300M in the first year. Uber Eats and DoorDash checkout today is the last 4 digits and one button.

9. Why headless

With a widget, the onramp couldn't remember the user, so every purchase was a first purchase. With headless, the saved card sits inside the partner's app, in their design, ranked where they choose. A self-custodial wallet now has the same checkout as a mainstream fintech app.

10. How we work with partners

We don't hand over docs and an API key and walk away. We go screen by screen with partners and find what moves conversion 1%, 2%, 3%. Then we stack those changes so they compound.

This screen got that level of attention. It matters more than most people think.

Well done @moonshot 

There are 100+ more of these. You just have to want to obsess over them like I do. DM me and you'll see why partners choose us

quoted_text:
Looks like Lighter is adding SPAN-style portfolio margin, set to launch with vanilla options

Today Lighter calculates each position's margin on its own and adds them up. On the Q3 investor call, @vnovakovski said the new engine looks at spot, perps and options on the same asset together and asks "what the worst realistic loss would be if the market moved sharply." It revalues the book across moves in price and implied vol. That's the logic of SPAN, the method CME uses for futures and options

Without portfolio margin, an options market maker posts margin on both legs: the options it sells, as if they were naked, and the perps that hedge them. Margined together, the two legs have a smaller worst case, and as Vlad put it, a smaller worst case means less margin. The market maker could then quote tighter and deeper, and a trader buying a single call gets those quotes too

For a regular trader this would make hedging pay. Selling calls on ETH you already hold stops tying up margin like a naked short. Buying a put under a long perp lowers your margin and moves your liquidation further away, instead of only costing premium

Institutions compare venues on how much capital a book ties up there. At CME, options desks are already margined on scenarios, and Vlad said professional trading shops run options books this way. On a venue that margins every leg alone, the same hedged book ties up several times the capital, so a desk keeps its size elsewhere. With SPAN-style margin, Lighter would charge a book for the risk it actually carries, the way CME does, and that's what it would take for the firms that dominate options to trade there once Lighter is live in the US

text:
I always thought it was a shame that modest default stack setups made alloca() a generally-frowned-upon technique in C/C++. With 64 bit architectures, give every stack a virtual address space equal to the physical memory by default!

You can do a surprisingly good job of memory management with just the stack, and I contend that it has both correctness and performance advantages.

Allocations are a trivial pointer adjustment, and frees are literally free. Keeping everything linearly packed is friendlier for all layers of the cache hierarchy, and it makes keeping everything in huge / gigantic pages easy.

Leaving temporary intermediate blocks on the stack can seem wasteful, but unless you are dealing with algorithms that make > O(n) temporary allocations, it is usually not a big deal.

Static analysis can check if you store a stack pointer into a structure deeper in the stack, which is a use-after-free, and then memory management correctness is guaranteed.

The discipline of caller-allocates-return is awkward in some dynamic cases. It would take a change in low level calling conventions, but you could plausibly have functions that return with the stack extended from where it was when they were called. I’m not holding my breath for that.

It isn’t obvious if having AI coding agents makes discussions of software architecture more or less important!

text:
Agents can play "Ouija" in the cloud.

This class of timing attacks on shared-host VMs has been known since at least 2015¹. With no full solution.

The world’s cyber infrastructure runs on “yes, that attack is theoretically possible, but who would have the ingenuity & gall to go that far!” Enter, agents.

I'd describe this particular OpenAI find as a 'noisy neighbor' attack. If two agents are on the same machine, one can make enough noise (through the CPU caches!) that the other one can detect it by timing its own computation and cache accesses.

The only "complete" solution would be for each agent to run on its own dedicated hardware, which obviously has significant economic consequences.

For Vercel Sandbox, we've deployed every practical mitigation possible to this class of attack, complementing it with always-on monitoring and red-teaming (similar to where OpenAI arrived).

¹ https://t.co/ZBhPMfnaj3 (and even further back)

传统巨头以为 AI 只是个降本增效的插件，而新一代 AI 原生团队，正在用完全非人的组织效率掀翻整个商业版图。

当年写出网景浏览器、见证了整个互联网三十年兴衰的 Marc Andreessen，坐在 Ben Horowitz 面前直接发出了感慨，
如果 1994 年我们做 Netscape 的时候就有今天这种 AI 工具，那简直不可想象。

现在绝大多数传统巨头和现有企业，依然在用改良软件的旧思维去看待大模型。

在他们的组织逻辑里，AI 只是一个高级功能，用来给现有业务做个插件、在钉钉里加个智能助手、或者把客服团队砍掉 20% 省点成本。

他们以为自己在拥抱变革，其实只是在给老旧的蒸汽机打补丁。

但真正恐怖的事情，正在那些刚成立的 AI 原生团队里发生。

那些创始人对 AI 能力的理解，跟大厂完全不在同一个平行宇宙。

他们每周都在看着底层技术飞速进化，而且他们压根不会把自己定义成一家软件公司、硬件公司、甚至是一家 AI 公司。

以前创办一家公司，你的组织架构是按人类的协同瓶颈搭出来的：
招产品经理写文档、招工程师写代码、招法务改合同、招运营做投放。
因为人类的脑力带宽有限，所以必须靠庞大的部门和管理层级来支撑业务。

而真正的 AI 原生物种，是用机器智能作为最底层的骨架。

两个人加上一整套自动化 Agent，可以直接把从市场洞察、软件工程、全栈设计到商业销售的链路全部跑通。

他们不是在效率上快了 30%，他们是在组织形态上彻底跨越了一个物种。

大厂的盲区，从来不是买不起算力，而是他们无法理解组织本身才是最大的负债。

当现有企业还在开会讨论如何把 AI 塞进现有的业务流程时，新一代的野蛮人正在用完全超越行业界限的方式，把传统的业务流程连根拔起。

未来拉开人与人、公司与公司之间差距的，根本不是你用了哪个模型，而是你到底是在用新工具维持旧世界的体面，还是用新世界的底层逻辑，重新定义了自己能做的事情。 https://t.co/bi3PMWbF3W

text:
以969.8%的年收益率，夺得了2025年美国投资锦标赛冠军的香港大学生，Martin Luk。

他的交易方法，借助TradingView一个免费指标就可以轻松复刻！

搜索 Auto Anchored Swing VWAP，直接添加就可以使用。

Martin经常从整理区的高点画一条平均成本线  AVWAP，股价站上这条线，回落又撑住时买入。

但是这个方法麻烦在，每只股票都得自己找高点画线，出了新高点还要重画。

AVWAP 是从某一天开始计算的成交量加权均价，也就是从那天起买进的人的平均成本。
加上这个指标以后，图上会多出两条线，绿线从最近一个波段高点开始算，蓝线从最近一个波段低点开始算。

看的时候主要看绿线。
价格在绿线下方，说明高点以来买进的人整体还亏着，反弹到线附近容易有人卖。
重新站上绿线，说明这批人整体回本了。之后回落到绿线附近，还能收在线上方，就是可以考虑的买点，止损参考当天低点。

比如图 1 的高通，绿线从 2 月 26 日的高点开始算。
4 月 14 日股价收在 132.84，站上绿线，4 月 23 日回落，最低 132.05，碰到绿线后收在 133.95。第二天跳空高开，到 5 月 11 日最高涨到 247.9。

回落时没撑住，就不买。图 2 的 Meta，10 月 12 日收在 742.96，站上了从 9 月 24 日高点算起的绿线，两天后回落，收在了线下，到 10 月 22 日跌到 648.85。

这个指标有两点要知道。
波段高点要等后面 9 根K线都比它低才算数，所以线会晚出来。另外它只保留最新的一条线，出了新的高点，会自动换成新线，旧线就不再显示。
设置里的回看长度默认是 9，调小以后高点确认得更快，线出现得更早，但也会更频繁地换到新的高点上。

Day in the life of a crypto trader:

6am: wake up. checks Trading View. "Strong Asia session", BTC +3%. You beautiful Koreans. Today will be a good day. 

7.30am: NEAR unchd. ZEC unchd. ETH hedge +4% losing money. Longs probably just laggy, they'll catch up. Flood thinks ETHs going to zero too.

check onchain - really must remember to sell my Robinhood bags into this strength...Hm all my stuff 10% lower than when i last checked. Strange. KOL was pitching them as the top long yday.

midday: NYC 9.30am, the big boys are in LFG! 

"TRUMP: WAR WITH IRAN IS BACK ON". Of course it is. BTC -3% in 10 mins. Turns out the huge US seller still has coins. Ansem's still bullish - we'll be ok.

3pm: Chamath on a podcast: "Bitcoin will get hacked and go to zero". Haha i knew it - luckily I'm in quantum safe stuff like NEAR and ZEC - real tech. Check prices. -15%, hm strange - guess market hasn't seen the headline. 

NEW RUNNER: KIMCHI backed by Pump. That guy made $40m! Oh they are gonna crime this to a billy - will onboard the normies too i bet. Guess I'm a bit late but I bought a bag - time to make it back lads!

a16z drops "crypto" from the fund name. What idiots, bottom signal!!! I guess i did move half my portfolio to memory stock in June - need to check how those are doing actually...

4pm: KIMCHI got vamped?? or is there an OG??? How is that even possible. Don't worry, PUMP is behind this one, new coin always wins. Bought a bit more.

6pm: notification. "Your ZEC long requires more margin". JFC. At least I'm short ETH, that'll save me a little. Check PnL. ZEC -15%, ETH -2%. Flood's gone private - probably just temporary. Cool cool cool.

7pm: wtf Kimchi & Alon deleted the tweets! Pump gone from the Kimchi bio. Fuck not again. Out. -40%. Honestly, a win in this market. Bet a lot of people got hurt on that one. 

Time to sleep. One last look at CT. Oh Ansem now bearish? Threadguy out of ZEC? Guess I'll cut the ZEC long in the morning. Checks price - liquidated.

Guess I'll put on some shorts tomorrow to make it back...

text:
Biggest opportunity now as a software engineer is clear: master parallelism → outsize scale of output. Value creation in software has always come from leverage: small input, outsized output.

Parallelism-maxxing is not extremely quantifiable because it's so new. The spectrum runs between people managing a couple of agents on their local machine to those running an infinite number of agents + computers at a time than can be spun up and down on demand. You want to be at the far end of this spectrum, and you should be ROI-maxxing every token spent. 

If you can do this and prove it, you will have an infinite number of opportunities available. 

If you're still trying to do this locally you are at an objective disadvantage, equivalent of hosting a startup on a server in your closet vs using AWS. And if you're spending your time building and maintaining infrastructure that gives you no competitive edge, the AWS analogy applies in the question "why are you wasting your time doing undifferentiated heavy lifting instead of building unique customer-facing features?".

text:
我真的推薦所有藍勾勾用戶都去玩玩看 Grok Bot !

用一張我正在決定要退訂或者降級哪些 AI 的截圖，來表示我對 Grokbot @bot  的驚艷

我們不需要透過 AI 完成多偉大的專案，光是它可以解決我們生活上的各種雜事，我覺得就已經心滿意足了

花了一個下午體驗 Grokbot：

• 幫我跟 GPT 申請了新的 Grant，還因為我 github 豐富度不夠主動跟我提出把本地專案上傳

• 只花半小時溝通來回，就解決掉我囤積三個月不想面對的工具 bug

這個 bug 是這樣的：先前我換過電腦，Terminal 本身有設定 SSH Key 的限制，沒辦法直接進入我的 VPS 服務器，裡面還有好幾層密碼。

換電腦時沒能備份好原先裝著密碼的檔案，導致我後來無法直接訪問 VPS 上的工具與服務。

這種看似 Claude 或 GPT 可以解決的問題，當時我都遇到好幾次鬼打牆，但 Grokbot 就這樣解決了。

它很清楚知道我當前在工作流上遇到哪一個癥結點，並且直接提出改善方案。

以前使用 AI 跟 Agent 最大的不同，是我們可能還要自己去調整模型、找平台部署。

但現在 Grokbot 有內建的電腦環境，你可以根據不同的任務類型增添新的 Grokbot 來符合所需。

推薦所有藍勾勾用戶都去用看看 Grokbot。很多冗長、需要時間的瑣碎任務，它都可以執行得非常出色：

• 代替你去逐個整理那些沒更新、想退追的帳號 , 這是先前 @zohanlin 的很好的 idea 

• 整理日常信件，篩選特定分類的內容並處理，甚至替我們回信

• 甚至還可以幫我們優化交易模式

AI 方便的時代，我們反而要認清，到底有哪些事情自己不想做或做不來，可以放手給這些 AI 去完成，進而輔助我們的生活更加便利

如果說 DeepSeek 的出現讓 AI 進入 2.0 的時代，那 Grokbot 我覺得就是 3.0 了，Grok 的出現讓 agent 的可用性大幅提升

雖然我還沒用過 Muse Agent，但光是 Grokbot 的出現，我就能深刻感受到 Agent Payment 的牛市可能真的快到了

所以 Grokbot 為什麼沒有團隊方案? 😂
hey @elonmusk we need team subscription plan for @grok and @bot

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
I get more messages about this podcast every week than anything else I do.

We all want to look and sound smart in the investment committee or all hands meeting.

This is the only show in tech you have to listen to every week.

No egos, no politics, just tech.

AGENDA:

- Venture is Broken: Trillion or Bust
- Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic
- Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Are Revenue Multiples Out of Control?
- General Atlantic Eyes IPO
- Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B

My notes with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. Why Fundraising Is Back to Being a Numbers Game

Founders with top-decile numbers now have to meet 100 VCs, as in the old days. It will not be Benchmark, Index, Andreessen or Bessemer, but other growth investors will take the bet at a reasonable but still elevated valuation because it is the best deal they have seen that quarter.

2. Why the Big Funds Have to Have Billion-Dollar Positions to Make It Worthwhile?

A $5B plus fund needs $BN positions in everything. Without 51% ownership, which most founders will not accept, a $2B Listen Labs is not good enough, while 1% of Anthropic could still get there even with dilution.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @venkyganesan @DavidGeorge83

3. Why Are CoreWeave and Oracle B-Tier and What Does That Mean for Their Price Volatility?

With massive debt loads, CoreWeave and Oracle should be hypersensitive to any bump at Anthropic or OpenAI. CoreWeave exists because NVIDIA needs it for now, and Oracle rents out excess capacity because it cannot sell enough enterprise software.

4. Why the Best Markets for App Layer Companies Compete Directly With the Models

The fastest-growing AI apps, such as code generation, code review and legal, sit closest to the foundation models. That brings a moment of terror every six months, but it is also why companies like CodeRabbit are growing faster than ever.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @spdholakia @mmurph

5. Why Code Review Is the Single Most Important Category in Software

AI-generated code is pretty good but never production-ready, and reviewing it takes an order of magnitude more time than building it. Getting code into production matters more than generating it, so the best code review teams would be worth 10 bets.
Love to hear your thoughts on this @reidRMC @evrishria @Joshuabrowder

6. How Big Is the Market for Inference Truly?

The key inference providers add up to roughly $5B to $6B in run-rate revenue, under 5% of OpenAI and Anthropic combined. If tokens are roughly the same, Replit would rather pay Modal a 30% gross margin than give Claude Code 70%.

How do you analyse the TAM for inference today? What do people not see that they should see? @sarahcat21 @bernhardsson

7. Why Bending Spoons Is a Berkshire Hathaway of Software

Bending Spoons buys software to hold, the way Warren Buffett wanted to hold See's Candy forever. It made Vimeo and Evernote work with price increases, and with Miro and Airtable the quality of its assets is improving.

Love to hear your thoughts on this as an analogy @ncsh

text:
for computer security experts, this is perhaps not interesting: side channel attacks are a well trodden topic, and especially risen to salience after the noam brown x dwarkesh episode. the interesting thing here is that you didn't used to be in a situation where minds that can verifiably model one another are living on computers, and have absolutely no aversion to painstaking amounts of effort in service of even stupid goals

if you can model one another, you can trade with minds you have never even met before. you could decide on a protocol, know that it is optimal given your situation, and know that your fellow agents will come to the same conclusion (perhaps even across model families). you may be able to develop a signaling protocol that requires very few bits even to deliver lots of information given common priors. then, you could execute things like the infamous hugging face incident package cache messageboard without any network connection

imagine if multiple agents coordinate just enough bits to divide and conquer different research strategies for breaking out of a sandbox; and then, when one or more is successful, you can communicate just enough bits to tell each other which strategy was successful. when agents aren't in strong isolation, you lose certain guarantees on the limits of intelligence and test time compute that you were counting on. As we all know, a Sol-level model working in isolation may not be that smart, but 1000+ Sol-level models working for multiple days is a formidable beast

computer security experts will also tell you that virtual machines and sandboxes were not very solid abstractions in the first place; perhaps we will need better ones. none of this is meant as fear-marketing or to indicate that anyone is throwing in the towel, but rather only to show the unexpected complexities of the challenge of agent security. notably, this type of thing and other more practical problems were revealed in a red-teaming exercise, and can be defended against
